World.title: Belarus joins Russia’s war on freedom of information
World.content:
Belarus' decision to ban the Euronews website by designating it as “extremist” and adding it to its “Republican List of Extremist Materials” marks a new escalation by authorities in Minsk in their crackdown on independent media and free speech.

 

The Belarus Ministry of Information’s move, reported by Belarus-based media, resulted in the immediate restriction of access to Euronews’ digital platforms in the country’s territory, as shown by Euronews’ real-time traffic-monitoring systems.

As of Saturday, Belarus has still not communicated its decision to Euronews, which was reportedly taken on 4 August - nor has it outlined the reasoning behind it.

The Ministry of Information had already banned Euronews’ television broadcasts in April 2021 following its coverage of nationwide protests against Belarusian leader Aliaksandr Lukashenka.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko speaks to journalists during a joint press conference with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto at Merdeka Palace in Jakarta. AP Photo

The Belarus government's official argument then was that Euronews’ broadcasting license had expired and that the channel was publishing adverts in English rather than translating them into Russian or Belarusian in line with local laws.

Euronews was also not notified of that decision and once again learned of the ban through media outlets in Belarus.

In a statement published after the 2021 ban came into effect, Euronews condemned the decision and said that it would "do its utmost to ensure that its audiences in Belarus can very soon again have access, on television, to its hallmark impartial and quality journalism."

"In the meantime, these audiences will be able to continue following us on our digital platforms," it added.

Following in Russia's footsteps

Euronews had built a significant audience in Belarus and in Russia over the years, its digital traffic data shows.

However, Moscow decided to ban Euronews’ television and digital platforms across Russia in March 2022, shortly after it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as Euronews refused to comply with the censorship and propaganda-driven measures imposed by the Kremlin on the media.

Russian President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister - Presidential Envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District Yury Trutnev at the Kremlin in Moscow. Sputnik

The decision to stop broadcasting Euronews was taken by Russia’s audio-visual regulator Roskomnadzor following a request from the Prosecutor General’s Office. It threatened Euronews with “criminal liability” and accused the outlet of publishing “unreliable information on a special military operation being carried out by the Russian Armed Forces, as well as information containing calls for people to participate in mass (public) events.”

After Russian President Vladimir Putin's troops invaded Ukraine, the Kremlin told the media not to call its full-scale invasion a war, while also issuing other directives that contravened Euronews’ fundamental editorial values.

Responding at the time, Euronews rejected “the allegations of 'fake news' and of calling citizens to protest”.

“We firmly condemn this intolerable restriction imposed on the millions of people across Russia who relied on Euronews, more than ever, to get impartial fact-based news, in a context of heightened disinformation and propaganda,” Euronews said in a statement.

Russian authorities continued to criminalise the dissemination of what it called information “discrediting” the Russian army and threatened journalists with up to 15 years in prison.

More recently, Euronews revealed that multiple fake news videos were being posted on Russian social media copying the publication's journalistic and visual style in an attempt to spread false political information.

These come as part of a wider, sophisticated fake news campaign targeting Western media and European societies.

Belarus, Russia and Iran’s media crackdown

Minsk's decision mirrors a series of similar measures taken by Moscow in clamping down on internet platforms it does not fully control.

On the same day that Belarus took the decision to ban Euronews’ digital platforms, the Kremlin blocked dozens of VPN services used by Russians to bypass internet restrictions, in a move that experts described as one of the largest crackdowns on VPN services in recent years.

Russia has repeatedly imposed restrictions on media outlets, as well as social media channels and foreign technology companies, since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In July 2025, Moscow also imposed legislation criminalising "searching for extremist content online."

In August 2025, Russian authorities announced they were “partially” restricting calls through Telegram and WhatsApp messaging applications, in a further effort to tighten control over the internet.

Since the beginning of 2026, the Kremlin has moved to fully block Telegram and WhatsApp across Russia, triggering some of the most significant pushback from Kremlin supporters in the four years since the invasion of Ukraine.

The Iranian government has also followed Russia’s lead, blocking all internet access across Iran in response to anti-regime protests in January 2026. It has continued the ban throughout the Iran war.

In recent months, Tehran has introduced additional internet controls and severe penalties for VPN usage, while designating certain media publications as enemies of the state.

World.title: Tisza Party group nominates András Baka for new Hungarian president
World.content:
András Baka is an internationally recognised legal scholar, who began his career at the Institute for Legal Studies of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, then became director general of the College of Public Administration. The peak of his international judicial career came when he served for two terms, between 1991 and 2008, as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) in Strasbourg. On his return home, in 2009, parliament elected him president of the Supreme Court. The second Orbán government, which came to power in 2010 with a constitution-making majority, removed him by renaming the Supreme Court as the Curia, thereby formally creating a new institution and appointing a new head to lead it.

 

Baka subsequently won a case against the Hungarian state at the European Court of Human Rights, which found that his rights to a fair trial and to freedom of expression had been violated. He has been a regular voice on rule-of-law issues in Hungary and abroad. He is an independent-minded, somewhat old-school lawyer, and Hungary has had several presidents of this type. His ability to embody national unity may be complicated by the fact that he has been an outspoken critic of the Orbán system both at home and internationally.

Powerless presidents instead of symbols of national unity

Before the elections, Tisza Party leader Péter Magyar had already indicated that, if they secured a constitution-making majority, they would remove most of the high public dignitaries appointed by Fidesz, with the exception of central bank governor Mihály Varga. He argued that these dignitaries were loyal Fidesz party foot soldiers who had failed to fulfil their constitutional duties and whose aim after the election would be to obstruct the work of the Tisza government.

In the Hungarian system the president of the republic primarily plays a ceremonial role and has little independent political room for manoeuvre. Under Fidesz rule, however, the presidents did not use even this limited legal and communicative space, instead operating in parallel with the government and cooperating with it in every respect.

During the period of government from 2010 to 2016, only János Áder, a political veteran of the party, managed to serve the two terms available to him in full.

László Sólyom, who had been elevated to the post by Fidesz while it was still in opposition and who projected an independent political and legal profile, was not elected for a second term. His successor, Pál Schmitt, a former Fidesz vice president, fell over a plagiarism scandal. János Áder then became president, and after his second term he was followed by Katalin Novák.

Novák spent her entire political career in Fidesz, but as a young woman she was officially meant to show a more European, more Western-facing face of the party than the mainstream led by Viktor Orbán. She had to step down after the pardon for sex abuse scandal. At that point Tamás Sulyok was elected, a figure little known to the public and without a strong public profile, and he too did not complete his first term.

President Tamás Sulyok was ultimately removed by means of a short sentence inserted into the 17th constitutional amendment, which the lawyer elected by Fidesz signed, thereby ending his mandate.

Tisza has indicated that it will adopt a new constitution within this parliamentary term and will at least consider the possibility of electing the president of the republic directly.

Tisza's first political misstep

Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised public consultation on the choice of president, then, after a very short time, announced that the parliamentary group was nominating women's world chess champion Judit Polgár. The announcement was followed by a strong outcry; critics of the decision argued that the absence of consultation cast a shadow over the selection process. Sensing the outrage, Polgár declined Magyar's offer. After the failed nomination, Medián, one of Hungary's most trusted pollsters, measured the first significant drop (3–5 percentage points) in support for Tisza, which nevertheless remained at a historically high level, at 68% among decided party voters.

Tisza chose Baka from three candidates; the other two were historian Ignác Romsics and independent lawyer Botond Fülöp, who publishes under the pseudonym Vidéki Prókátor and was the one who brought to light the pardon case that led to President Katalin Novák's resignation.

World.title: Around 34,000 fans attend Kanye West concert at Algarve Stadium
World.content:
The concert in Portugal went ahead despite pressure for it to be cancelled, as has happened on his tour in other countries. Australia even refused the US rapper a visa. The same happened in the United Kingdom. Other European countries, including France, Poland, Italy and Czechia, have cancelled West's tour, also known as Ye.

 

In Portugal, the Israeli ambassador was the most prominent public voice calling for the rapper's concert to be cancelled, but that did not happen. The show at the Estádio do Algarve went ahead on Friday and, according to what has been reported by various media outlets (source in Portuguese) and on social networks, everything went smoothly.

A winner of 24 Grammys (source in Portuguese), Kanye West is one of the most awarded artists in Grammy history, alongside Jay-Z, the most decorated hip-hop artist. West took to the stage at the Estádio do Algarve 45 minutes after the scheduled start time.

Standing on top of a giant globe on the pitch, Ye performed well-known tracks such as "Stronger", "Gold Digger", "American Boy" and "I Can't Wait", invited his daughter North West on stage for a duet and did not make any controversial remarks or speeches, as he has done in recent years.

This was the third time the US rapper has performed in Portugal. His debut came in 2006, at Cool Jazz in Oeiras, and the second in 2011, at the Sudoeste Festival in Zambujeira do Mar.

Kanye West's international tour, which is promoting his 12th album, "Bully", has been surrounded by controversy, largely because of the antisemitic hate speech he has previously adopted and his declarations of support for Nazism.

"Someone who has glorified Hitler, promoted antisemitism and claimed that slavery was a choice, a phrase that deeply offended millions of descendants of the victims of slavery. This is not provocation, it is hate speech," said the Israeli ambassador in Lisbon, Oren Rozenblat, when he took to social media to call for the concert to be cancelled, arguing that such a show would be a "disgrace for Portugal and for the Portuguese".

In a full-page  in the Wall Street Journal (source in Portuguese), the rapper sought to make amends by apologising for the antisemitic comments he made in the past. West described his behaviour as "a four-month manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behaviour" and said he "lost touch with reality".

The Algarve concert was never the subject of public or media outrage in Portugal. The organiser of the event in Portugal told Euronews it was 'a non-issue', driven by 'misinformation', even suggesting it was turning into 'a political issue' when it should not be. "It is a musical event that is going to take place," said the CEO and co-founder of Raya Culture in April. "It would only become a [political] issue if the authorities identified a national threat to public order, which is not the case," he stressed.

But Kanye's stance is not confined to antisemitism or hate speech.

The US rapper has shared, on social networks and at public events, episodes involving his wife, Bianca Censori, that have been regarded as deplorable and sexist.

Among the many controversies, Kanye "Ye" West has been at the centre of several recent legal cases, including complaints from former staff accusing him of abuse, as well as a lawsuit filed by a former assistant who accuses him of sexual assault and alleges that he strangled a model on the set of a music video in 2010.

After the concert in the Algarve, Kanye West is due to perform in Kazakhstan, at the Central Stadium in Almaty (14 August), before returning to the United States for two concerts. The first is in New Orleans on 28 August, followed by Chicago on 3 September 2026.

World.title: US intends to send $1 billion in aid to Colombia following de la Espriella's inauguration
World.content:
The US State Department said on Friday that it planned to announce a $1 billion security package for new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella's right-wing administration.

 

In a press release, the office of the spokesperson for the department said the package aimed to help Washington and Bogotá achieve "our shared goals."

De la Espriella was sworn in as president on Friday in a ceremony attended by a US delegation that included acting attorney general Todd Blanche.

"The delegation demonstrates U.S. commitment to reinvigorating the U.S.-Colombia relationship and deepening of our shared security and economic partnership," the State Department said.

US President Donald Trump has been highly complimentary of de la Espriella, calling him a "smart, strong, and tough leader" that he predicted would be "tremendously successful" as president of Colombia and as a ballast for the right in the South American nation. Trump previously said de la Espriella would have the "total support and strength of the United States behind him" in office.

On Friday, Washington said Colombia had also now joined the "Shield of the Americas," an alliance of governments stretching from the US across Central and South America that has vowed to fight narcotrafficking groups.

"The Trump Administration welcomes Colombia joining the Shield of the Americas and stands ready to support the de la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten U.S., Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity," the State Department said.

The US has become increasingly involved in Latin America during Trump's second term in the White House, carrying out strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats coming from the region and launching an operation to capture former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. Maduro has since been held in custody in New York on charges including narco-terrorism and drug trafficking - to which he has pleaded not guilty.

World.title: Rome-Madrid row: how Spain checks travellers arriving from Italy
World.content:
A full-blown row has erupted between Rome and Madrid after the Meloni government refused to accept the Spanish cabinet's ultimatum to lift border checks for people arriving in Italy from Spain. From Saturday morning, travellers entering Spain from Italy will be subject to the same measures introduced by the government in Rome on 1 August.

 

According to the information available, Spanish border checks will remain in place until 7 September, while on Friday the Italian government reiterated that the suspension of the Schengen agreement will remain in force at least until 15 August.

At the height of the holiday season, with thousands of people travelling between Italy and Spain and trips already booked, Madrid's retaliatory move is likely to cause confusion at airports and ports. It is a situation which, the authorities in Madrid have complained, Spanish citizens have already experienced on arriving in Italy, where they have been subjected to the checks imposed by Rome.

How border checks work in Spain

The Spanish government has explained that citizens arriving from Italy by air, sea or land may be subject to checks from midnight on Saturday 8 August. Travellers from the European Union will be asked to show an identity document, while non-EU nationals will also have to present a visa or residence permit.

Italian citizens can present a passport or a national identity card valid for travel abroad, but this must be in electronic format (CIE), because since 3 August 2026 paper identity cards have no longer been valid as travel documents.

Related Spain to introduce retaliatory border checks on travellers from Italy

Where checks are carried out

Identity document checks could lead to queues and delays, especially at the busiest hubs such as Madrid and Barcelona.

At airports, travellers may be checked at arrival gates or at boarding. For those arriving by sea, checks may be carried out at embarkation or during disembarkation. People entering Spain from Italy by car, after crossing France, may be stopped at the French-Spanish border crossing and asked to show their identity documents.

What to do when travelling with children or animals

Citizens travelling with children must ensure that minors also have identity documents. In Italy, documents are valid for three years up to the age of three, and for five years up to the age of 18. In addition, children under 14 are not allowed to travel alone. To travel to Spain with pets, an EU pet passport is required, issued by a vet, with identification via microchip and a valid rabies vaccination.

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: US Senate confirms Trump loyalist Todd Blanche as new AG
World.content:
Republicans dropped their opposition and confirmed President Donald Trump's former defense lawyer to a Cabinet position. Now, Todd Blanche will act as the nation's top law enforcement officer.

The US Senate has narrowly approved President Donald Trump's nominee for the job of attorney general, making Todd Blanche the nation's top law enforcement officer in an early morning vote on Saturday.

The Republican-controlled body delivered a 50-49 vote to confirm the controversial Trump loyalist.

Louisiana Republican Bill Cassidy was the last-minute convert this time, supplying the crucial deciding vote after his colleagues Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine jumped ship to join the chamber's Democrats in voting against Blanche's appointment.

In explaining her opposition, Murkowski said the country was in need of an attorney general "who will check the worst impulses of this administration."

On the Senate floor, Cassidy outlined his own conversion, saying he believed Blanche's relationship with Trump would make him effective at pushing back against Trump's demands.

Blanche, a former federal prosecutor who was Trump's personal defense lawyer and had been serving as acting attorney general since April, wrote on X, "I am deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation's 88th attorney general."

Senators question whether Blanche will be nation's lawyer, or Trump's

There is great concern that Trump sees Blanche as "his lawyer," something that he has often openly expressed the need for in the position of attorney general, which is supposed to be independent.

"The attorney general is supposed to be the people's lawyer," Illinois Democratic Senator Dick Durbin said during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday.

"Mr. Blanche," added Durbin, the Committee's ranking Democrat, "continues to operate as the president's personal lawyer, treating the Justice Department like a law firm serving one client — the president."

On Saturday, Durbin said it would be a "serious mistake" to give Blanche control at the DOJ, "If there is ever a moment in history when we need an attorney general above reproach, who is clearly dedicated to ending corruption, even at the highest level of our government, it's right now."

During his time in office, Trump has often railed against attorneys general for not being aggressive enough in pursuing his agenda — most often when it is tied to retribution against his political opponents.

Jeff Sessions, Bill Barr and Pam Bondi all fell out of the president's good graces for failing to fully satisfy his legal desires.

Blanche is seen as a staunch ally who has no qualms doing the president's bidding.

Epstein files: Expert warns release may shield 'Trump camp' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Blanche won votes by promising to scrap '1776 fund' and Trump tax immunity scheme

Blanche previously defended Trump against criminal charges over the falsification of business records with the intent of hiding an affair with an adult movie actress, as well as another for the mishandling of classified documents in his attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.

Both cases were dropped after Trump won reelection in 2024.

Blanche's visibility rose when he defended Trump in a so-called 'hush-money trial' centered on his falsification of business records to hide an affair Image: Sarah Yenesel/Pool/REUTERS

During his time at the DOJ, Blanche has handled portions of the case against deceased sex offender and presidential friend Jeffrey Epstein — most prominently overseeing the release of millions of documents tied to the case, as well as the transfer of Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell to a more comfortable, minimum-security federal prison in Texas after he personally met with her.

Under Blanche and his predecessor Bondi, the DOJ has lost thousands of employees through firing, resignation or voluntary departure.

Blanche's candidacy was vehemently opposed by Democrats, and even some Republican lawmakers had qualms with his avoidance of forthright answers about a dubious $1.776 billion (€1.5 billion) compensation fund for presidential political allies — including those who stormed the US Capital on January 6, 2021 — accusing the federal government of unfair treatment; and DOJ directives that would see the president, his two eldest sons and the Trump Organization shielded from tax audits and penalties for life.

Two retiring Republican senators, John Cornyn (Texas) and Thom Tillis (North Carolina), had loudly proclaimed that they would vote against Blanche's appointment unless the compensation fund was dropped.

He assured them that it would be, while also saying that the Trumps' tax immunity would only be applied "retroactively" and not to future filings, clearing the way for Saturday's confirmation vote.

World.title: Iran war: IRGC says Hormuz to open if US accepts Iran's terms
World.content:
08/08/2026 August 8, 2026 Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defense deal raises new security questions

On Friday, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan unveiled a new security alliance that bears strong similarities to NATO's principles of collective defense.

The three regional powers — who are also strategic allies of the US and are all majority Sunni nations — have signed a defense pact that is "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

The deal is widely viewed as the three Sunni-majority nations' way of defending themselves against the rising threat from an increasingly hostile Iran, where Shiite Islam is the state religion.

The agreement could also be seen as a sign of shifting power dynamics in the region, as well as a way to hedge against an unreliable US, amid uncertainty over its long-term commitment to its role in enforcing security in the Gulf.

DW's Brent Goff spoke to experts Dania Thafer and Kamran Bokhari to learn more about what the new agreement means for the region and the US-Iran conflict.

World.title: War, terror, diplomacy: What if Israel takes Al-Aqsa Mosque?
World.content:
Reports from Jerusalem suggest that Israeli authorities are taking over one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque. If they do, experts say anything could happen, from war to terrorism to ending diplomatic ties.

The statement issued after this week's meeting in Jordan was blunt about what might happen next.

Israeli infringements on one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque in east Jerusalem, could lead to "a religious conflict with repercussions that will extend beyond the region and threaten regional and international peace and security," the foreign ministers of 10 countries belonging to the Arab League said after Wednesday's emergency meeting in Amman, Jordan. The statement was also signed by ministers from Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, and Malaysia.

Jordan's foreign minister called the meeting because of mounting evidence that the Israeli government is surreptitiously changing a decades-old agreement meant to ensure intercommunal peace at the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, an area of great religious significance to Muslims, Jews, and Christians.

"We warn that tampering with the status quo … could trigger a religious conflict that will reverberate beyond Palestine and Jordan into the whole Muslim world," Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi told the UK newspaper the Guardian before the meeting.

Israel's Foreign Ministry issued a response, saying the statement was inaccurate and Jerusalem "has never been more open and accessible to worshippers of all faiths."

Jews at Al-Aqsa: In 2015, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said 'Muslims pray on the Temple Mount, non-Muslims visit the Temple Mount' Image: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

Why is Al-Aqsa such a big issue?

Al-Aqsa is considered the third-holiest site in Islam, after Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia. The compound, also known as the Temple Mount, is also Judaism's holiest site — two Jewish temples are thought to have stood there — and it is also of significance to Christians for its biblical connections to Jesus Christ's life.

Al-Aqsa also bears a lot of political weight because the mosque is seen by many as the embodiment of Palestinian identity, a flashpoint in a city sought as the capital of any eventual Palestinian state.

Because of the site's importance, when Israel first occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, it was deemed in the interests of Israeli national security to keep allowing Muslims to worship there. Jews could only visit and would not be allowed to pray there. Instead Jewish visitors perform religious rituals at the wall below the mosque, known as the Western or Wailing Wall.

Jordan was also allowed to continue its century-old custodianship of the site, and today the mosque is administered by a religious trust called the Islamic Waqf, paid for by Jordan at about $20 million (€17 million) annually. Israeli authorities still take care of security there.

Muslims say the Prophet Muhammad ascended to heaven from Al-Aqsa Image: Mahmoud Illean/AP Photo/picture alliance

This delicate compromise is known as the "status quo." But recent reports indicate that the situation has been changing.

Residents of Jerusalem say dozens of mosque officials employed by Jordan have been prevented from entering Al-Aqsa this year.

The number of Muslim worshipers halved during 2025 , according to Jerusalem-based monitors. More Jewish worshipers are being allowed in and are increasingly overtly performing rituals, something forbidden for decades, including by Jewish religious authorities. The Times of Israel reported in January that police openly let Jewish visitors take printed prayer sheets onto the site for the first time.

In June, there were also reports of an Israeli-US plan to turn the mosque area into a "multifaith center," although US Secretary of State Marco Rubio later denied any knowledge of such a plan.

Why is this happening now?

This is not the first time that the governments of Muslim-majority countries and activists in Jerusalem have issued such warnings.

For decades, Jewish fringe groups, often referred to as the Temple Mount movement, have demanded that they be allowed to pray at the site. The most extremist of these groups say they want to demolish the mosque and construct a new Jewish temple.

At first they were mostly ignored, Jerusalem-based lawyer Daniel Seidemann wrote in 2025 . Seidemann is the founder of Terrestrial Jerusalem, an organization that tracks such developments in the city. But, he said, that "radical fringe" has become more mainstream. "Over time, the Temple Mount movements, backed by more than 100 rabbis associated with the settler movement in the West Bank, became more visible, more vocal and more provocative," Seidemann said.

"This crisis has been decades in the making," said Omar Rahman, a fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. "There's been an effort from religious extremists to destroy the Al-Aqsa Mosque since at least the 1980s, when plots to do that were uncovered. But those groups and those ideologies have gained more representation within the Israeli [parliament] Knesset today."

In July, thousands of Jews prayed at the Al-Aqsa compound in violation of the status quo agreement Image: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

An October 2025 report by the Ir Amim Association , which focuses on Israeli-Palestinian issues in Jerusalem, found that politicians, including from within Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's national-conservative Likud party, frequently break rules around the Al-Aqsa status quo but never face consequences from authorities.

"In practice, Netanyahu allows and normalizes grave breaches of the status quo," the association reported. Yet Netanyahu "continues to declare that his government remains committed to the status quo and nothing has changed."

What happens if erosion of Al Aqsa status quo continues?

"It would be very unwise to make any sort of prediction," Joost Hiltermann, a special adviser for the Middle East and North Africa at the Crisis Group think tank, told DW.

But, Hiltermann said, it's essential to consider that "while the fate of Jerusalem as a city may be an overriding Palestinian concern, the fate of the holy sites of Islam in Jerusalem is an abiding global Muslim concern. Not just for the Arab world but also for the largest Muslim countries: Indonesia, Pakistan, Bangladesh. So any Israeli attempt to change the status quo would face a global backlash."

In the past, changes have led to violence. In 2000, Ariel Sharon, an Israeli right-wing opposition leader at the time, visited Al-Aqsa — an event that was seen as one reason for the Palestinian uprising known as the Second Intifada. In 2017, when Israeli authorities erected cameras and metal detectors at the site, it led to deadly protests.

UNESCO has declared the Old City of Jerusalem, including the Temple Mount, a World Heritage site, so any changes could be interpreted as a breach of international law, observers say Image: Simon Beni/Middle East Images/picture alliance

One likely outcome of further infringements of the status quo would be major public protests in Muslim-majority countries. "While the Arab regimes would be reluctant to engage in any sort of confrontation with Israel, their publics will be outraged," Hiltermann said. "The regimes will have to manage that, and they will try to do so by launching vigorous criticism of Israel, not followed by any action — they've become very good at that. The same will be true for Indonesia and others. But all of them may have a hard time controlling domestic fury."

Rahman said the consequences of further Israeli infringement would depend on how radically things changed at Al-Aqsa. "It would trigger a fairly significant reaction, but the extent of it is hard to say," he said. "It could spark a catastrophic religious war or maybe just a diplomatic reaction, or maybe it simply adds to the well of grievance against Israel," he added.

Because Al Aqsa is so important in Islam, it could also make it hard for some countries to resist an upsurge in anti-Israel feeling, even if they might want to, he adds. For example, countries like Morocco and the United Arab Emirates that normalized relations with Israel might feel forced to reverse that.

Because of Al Aqsa's significance to Palestinian identity, the Gaza-based militant group Hamas often says it is defending the mosque. Extremist groups with an Islamist background have also used defense of Al Aqsa to recruit members.

Edited by: M Gagnon

World.title: Bulgaria: Unknown drone explodes near Romanian border
World.content:
A drone that entered Bulgaria's airspace exploded near the Romanian border and the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, the Bulgarian prime minister said.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said that a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace from the north and exploded near the Romanian border on Saturday morning.

According to the prime minister, there were no casualties or damage to infrastructure, as the drone exploded in a sunflower field 100 meters from the border with Romania. He noted that neither of the two neighboring countries had detected the drone.

Radev added that the incident occurred about 1,000 meters from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine.

"We will continue to monitor the situation and strengthen surveillance. Following this incident, we will also redeploy border police anti-drone detection and countermeasure capabilities from the border with Turkey to the border with Romania," Radev said.

What do we know about the drone?

Speaking after an extraordinary meeting of his Cabinet's security council, Radev did not specify where the drone came from or what type it was.

However, he said that it was believed that the drone was carrying a significant amount of explosives given the strength of the blast and the black smoke it produced.

When asked if the drone was civilian or military, Radev said that there was photographic evidence available. However, because the drone was damaged in the explosion, it was impossible to determine its type.

After analysing the debris, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was of a type "widely used by the Ukrainian military."

Radev said the drone was not detected in Bulgarian or Romanian airspace because such drones are difficult to detect due to their small size.

Russian drone hits Romanian apartment block To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Drone incidents on rise in EU countries

In recent months, there have been an increasing number of incidents involving drones in Eastern European countries that are both EU and NATO members and that support Ukraine in its four-and-a-half-year war against Russia's invasion.

The origin of the drone that exploded in Bulgaria and its potential connection to Russia or Ukraine are still unclear. Radev said that teams from the Bulgarian border police and the Ministry of Defense are working to determine the origin of the drone.

Bulgaria's Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said the incident would be raised at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council early next week.

Romania, which borders Ukraine, has faced frequent drone incursions, including crashes on its territory, such as a May incident in which a drone struck an apartment building.

Earlier this week in Germany, an explosive-laden drone was defused at Leipzig Airport, in what Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called a "new level of danger."

World.title: EU holds talks with big tech over Ceuta misinformation
World.content:
EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen has called for closer monitoring of social media platforms moving forward, amid the spread of misinformation during the recent migrant influx at Spain's Ceuta.

EU Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy Henna Virkkunen has called on social media giants to exercise closer monitoring of their platforms for misinformation, especially "during crisis situations."

Virkkunen was referring to last week's Ceuta border crisis, which European, Spanish and Moroccan authorities say was exacerbated by the spread of misinformation on social media, including TikTok, Telegram and Meta platforms.

Commissioner Virkkunen addressed the disinformation on social media, calling for greater EU monitoring of platforms during crisis situations.

"Platforms must act decisively in keeping the integrity of the digital space, in particular during crisis situations," she wrote on X.

"Monitoring must increase, cooperation with fact-checkers to be strengthened," Virkkunen wrote after a Friday meeting with representatives from TikTok and Meta — which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

Social media increasingly central to 'political debate'

A number of the estimated 72,000 people who stormed Ceuta from Morocco said they were attracted by false promises disseminated on social media and that they were lied to about the situation.

Spain and Morocco have also exchanged blame, with authorities in Rabat blaming a Spanish Supreme Court ruling that it says was exploited by human traffickers and misrepresented on social media.

Madrid says Morocco should have done a better job at stopping the tens of thousands of migrants who crossed the border.

Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the end, Spanish authorities say 80 people were killed during the course of events.

Moroccan authorities reported that 11 people died on their side of the border.

Rights groups estimate the total number of dead at more than 140.

The situation in Ceuta and the circumstances surrounding it have added more fuel to Europe's ongoing political fight over issues related to immigration and security.

Did misinformation on social media cause the Ceuta crisis?

In Ceuta, migrants pointed to social media messages and videos announcing that the EU border at Ceuta was suddenly open.

Why young Moroccans risked everything to reach Ceuta To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other posts informed people looking to get to the EU that accommodations would be available once they got to the Spanish territory and that they would be bused to the Spanish mainland from there.

Last week, EU member states convened an emergency meeting at which representatives mulled early-warning systems and social media monitoring as potential levers for improving the bloc's shared assessment capabilities in emerging situations.

Virkkunen said the EU would continue that discussion on Monday.

World.title: When German Catholics and Protestants share a church
World.content:
Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed in Germany. But there is a new, unique development.

From the outside, the Catholic church in Mannheim's Neuostheim district appears to be a typical 1950s church building: a relatively simple structure, nothing particularly remarkable about it. Yet St. Pius is truly unique. In this place of worship, Catholic and Protestant Christians celebrate services sharing the same space and taking turns in gathering around the same altar for Communion and the Eucharist.

"It actually began in the early 1970s," Annette Hübner, a Catholic parishioner, told DW. The 57-year-old has lived in the district with her family for more than half a century and is a member of the parish team. At the time, the parish priest of St. Pius was committed to fostering cooperation with the Protestant community and began holding ecumenical services in 1970. Then, at the end of 2009, the nearby Protestant St. Thomas Church sustained extensive water damage, and the building was found to be beyond repair.

What began as a temporary arrangement gradually evolved into a lasting solution. That lasting solution, in turn, grew into a genuine ecumenical friendship.

"It became increasingly clear that it made sense to continue working together," Hübner recalled. A banner on the facade of St. Pius proclaims: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." What may sound like a theological phrase from a Sunday sermon is part of everyday life here, on weekdays as much as on Sundays.

Annette Hübner feels that the Catholic and Protestant congretations in St.Pius are on a long journey that is well worth the effort Image: Christoph Strack/DW

Catholics and Protestants under one roof: Germany is home to 65 so-called Simultankirchen (shared churches). Their joint use was mandated by secular rulers soon after the Reformation and the resulting division of the Church. In some cases, detailed regulations even specified who was allowed to enter the church and at what times. The best-known examples are Altenberg Cathedral near Cologne and St. Peter's Protestant Cathedral in the eastern German city of Bautzen in Saxony.

In hospital and airport chapels, shared use by different Christian denominations is now almost taken for granted. A similar trend, however, is increasingly emerging in ordinary parish communities. Protestant and Catholic churches in Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia had already begun addressing the issue in 2017, during the commemorations marking the 500th anniversary of Martin Luther's Reformation.

"What If We All Moved In Together?" is the title of the Practical Guide to the Ecumenical Use of Churches and Parish Halls. The publication presents examples from the dioceses of Cologne and Aachen, as well as Essen, Münster and Paderborn.

The guide repeatedly points to the "accelerating reduction in church buildings." According to official church statistics for 2025, Germany had 24,500 Catholic and 21,100 Protestant churches, ranging from small chapels to grand cathedrals. Each year, dozens of churches are decommissioned, demolished or repurposed.

A new life for Germany's deconsecrated church buildings To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Attending a Protestant church was once considered 'a sin'

Examples of new shared church spaces can be found in both western and eastern Germany. In Schildow, on the northern outskirts of Berlin, only one church is expected to remain in use in the future: the larger and more prominent Protestant church. The Archdiocese of Berlin's press office describes the initiative as "an ecumenical project with exemplary character." Its statement also hints at the significance of this development: "For all the ecumenical openness that is now taken for granted," the Catholic participants still remember "earlier times when even attending a Protestant church was considered a sin."

Small congregations in the East

Catholic bishops in eastern Germany are quite accustomed to celebrating Mass in Protestant churches. For major occasions such as confirmations or parish anniversaries, the generally smaller Catholic churches are often unable to accommodate everyone. In such cases, their Protestant counterparts are often happy to provide the necessary space.

The German Bishops' Conference is also currently addressing the issue and plans to publish a practical guide on the subject. Here, too, the focus is on declining membership, church buildings that are no longer needed, financial constraints, and the potential for shared use.

St. Pius new altar was crafted from red and grey stone from the altar of two Protestant and Catholic Churches Image: Christoph Strack/DW

Two altars merged into one

But St. Pius in Mannheim is different. It is far more than a temporary arrangement born of necessity. Here, the two congregations have developed a deep and wide-ranging form of cooperation. Between 2020 and 2022, the church underwent extensive renovation and redesign. The place where the altar once stood is now occupied by the baptismal font, serving as a shared focal point for both churches. A new altar, crafted from red and grey stone, now stands in the nave.

"The red sandstone comes from the altar of the Protestant church, and the grey travertine from the altar of the Catholic church," Hübner explained. Both were crushed and cast together to form the new altar. Parts of its surface are completely smooth, while others remain rough, with visible grooves and fissures. "It was a beautiful symbol of the relationship between Protestants and Catholics. We want to come together. But there are still points of friction and unresolved questions."

Careful legal arrangements

St. Birgitta-Thomas Church in the northern German city of Kiel can likewise look back on decades of ecumenical cooperation. Since 1980, the Catholic parish of St. Birgitta and the Protestant Thomas congregation have shared both the church and the parish hall. Here, too, this "sharing" is governed by carefully defined legal arrangements.

Officially, the church belongs to the Catholic parish, while the parish hall belongs to the Protestant congregation. "But we use both parts of the complex jointly and on an equal footing," Pastor Rebekka Ulrich told DW. With a smile, she adds: "The Protestant side leased the printer, but the Catholic side uses it too."

The 36-year-old pastor sees "an incredible number of points of overlap." These include joint worship services, celebrations and ecumenical dialogue. Each year, the two denominations adopt a shared motto. A hymn of the month, selected alternately from the Protestant hymnal and the Catholic Gotteslob, is sung by the entire congregation during services.

In the ecumenical pastoral care center Emmaus in Bad Griesbach, Lower Bavaria, Protestants and Catholics share a common church space Image: Dietmar Stegmann

A shortage of clergymen and organists

The close partnership extends even to church music: both congregations share the same organist. "On Sundays, he accompanies the Catholic Mass at 9:30 a.m. and then the Protestant service at 11:00 a.m." If only everything were that simple. As Ulrich explains, the steadily declining number of Catholic priests is creating growing challenges for the Catholic side.

In Mannheim, Annette Hübner described the process as a journey that was long but, in her view, well worth the effort. The number of clergy is declining in both the Catholic and Protestant churches. At the local level, services of the Word conducted without a priest or pastor are becoming increasingly common.

Even the Eastern Christian tradition has found a place here. Since 1971, Mannheim has been home to the "Eastern Church Center Cyril and Methodius," which has been based at St. Pius from the very beginning. Once a month, a Catholic liturgy is celebrated according to the Byzantine Rite. Since the renovation, the church entrance area has included a specially designed space with icons and a symbolic iconostasis. All of this exists under a single church roof.

This article was translated from German.

08/08/2026 August 8, 2026 Demonstrations in Germany call for ban on far-right parties

Around 800 people demonstrated in Berlin, calling for the Federal Constitutional Court to review political parties suspected of right-wing extremism.

Eleven such demonstrations were planned across Germany on Saturday. The "Prüf," which translates to "check" or "examine," initiative, founded by activist Nico Semsrott, is behind the rallies.

Citing a legal opinion published in late June by the Society for Civil Rights that declared the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party unconstitutional, speakers called for a corresponding review by the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.

Many of the demonstrators' posters bore the slogan, "Examine today — protect tomorrow."

However, the Bundestag, the Bundesrat, or the federal government must file a motion to ban the party in order to initiate such a review.

In early May 2025, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution classified the AfD as a "confirmed far-right extremist movement," but suspended the designation after a legal challenge.

In February, a Cologne court said the agency can’t use the designation while the court evaluates the party’s lawsuit.

The AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism.

The Jharkhand government on Saturday held a second round of talks with various factions of the students protesting in Jharkhand over exam irregularities.

While the students said that the government heard their demands, they have decided to continue the protest until the issues are taken up with Chief Minister Hemant Soren before deciding whether to end their hunger strike.

The state government has held meetings with two different delegations of student protesters. Students from both factions have said they are prepared to march towards the Assembly on Monday.

The students are demanding the scrapping of the 14th Civil Services Preliminary Examination conducted by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) on July 2.

They are also seeking investigations by the Central Bureau of Investigation and the Enforcement Directorate into alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations conducted by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission.

World.title: Medio siglo del ‘Informe Hite’, el superventas que reveló la verdad sobre el orgasmo femenino y acabó con su autora en el exilio
World.content:
En 1976, la estadounidense Shere Hite saltó a la fama por la publicación de un libro que revelaba cómo las mujeres vivían su sexualidad y que una inmensa mayoría no llegaba al clímax durante el coito. Pese a su gran impacto, hoy sigue siendo difícil hacerse con un ejemplar

Entre los libros que han llegado a nuestros días de la ola feminista de los años setenta, El Informe Hite (1976) es uno de los menos conocidos. Pocas personas conocen el nombre de su autora, Shere Hite, nacida en Misuri en 1942, y el hito que representó que hace 50 años abriera el melón de que la mayoría de las mujeres no experimentaba orgasmos durante la penetración. Lo hizo en esta obra en la que recopilaba las respuestas de 3.000 mujeres de entre 14 y 78 años que, en algunos casos por primera vez, se expresaban libremente sobre su sexualidad. Trabajó durante cinco años en la compilación y síntesis de un volumen titánico de datos que ponían el foco en lo que realmente sentían las mujeres, denunciando una sexología hecha por y para hombres, centrada en el placer masculino y en la idea de penetración vaginal.

“Hite legitimó la experiencia femenina como una experiencia válida de conocimiento y abrió un debate que cambió la investigación sobre la sexualidad”, opina la sexóloga Ana Sierra. “Fue un auténtico cambio de paradigma. Desmontó la idea de que la penetración era el centro de la respuesta sexual femenina, y que si una mujer no alcanzaba el orgasmo de esa forma el problema estaba en ella. En realidad, puso de manifiesto que el modelo sexual dominante estaba incompleto”, añade. En el libro, Hite se alza contra el discurso histórico según el cual las mujeres tenían más dificultad para tener orgasmos que los hombres. “Mejor aún, se pretendía que una mujer incapaz de tener un orgasmo como un hombre durante el coito sufría simplemente un ‘bloqueo’ debido a un miedo psicológico o una neurosis (…) Erróneas y cargadas de prejuicios, estas ideas fijas han atravesado los siglos como tantas otras verdades intangibles”, escribe Hite.

El Informe Hite fue un éxito desde el principio, pese a los impedimentos de la editorial que, según cuenta su antigua editora en el documental Shere Hite y el orgasmo femenino (Nicole Newnham, 2023), dio la orden de no aceptar más de un cierto número de preventa, lo que limitaba automáticamente la tirada inicial del libro. Sin embargo, en pocos años fue traducido a más de una decena de idiomas y prohibido en una decena de países. Se estima que ha vendido unos 50 millones de ejemplares, lo que lo situaría entre los libros más vendidos de la historia.

Aun así, las violentas críticas de una parte del establishment y la contraofensiva reaccionaria y puritana que siguió a la revolución sexual en los setenta propiciaron que Hite acabara por autoexiliarse en Europa, agotada del clima mediático que la acosaba. Lo llamaban “el informe hate” (odio); decían que se estaba forrando criticando a los hombres y aseguraban que su trabajo buscaba en última instancia decir que las mujeres no necesitaban a los hombres en el sexo. Fue públicamente ridiculizada cuando salió a la luz que Hite había trabajado como modelo (posaba desnuda en ilustraciones para cine y literatura) para costearse los estudios de Historia, y sus métodos eran considerados poco científicos pese a que su estudio se basaba en una muestra de población mayor que la de muchos otros informes aplaudidos por la crítica. “Su metodología tenía limitaciones y la muestra no era representativa, pero eso no le resta valor histórico. Fue una investigación con un enorme peso cualitativo y sociológico, que abrió preguntas que después muchas investigaciones con metodologías más robustas han confirmado”, asegura Sierra.

Shere Hite con un ejemplar de su famoso libro en 1976. Bettmann Archive (via Getty Images)

Hite no era médico ni estaba diplomada en ciencias y su obra era puramente sociológica, pero su intuición puso el foco en cuestiones que quedaron confirmadas más adelante. Además, no perdió de vista el contexto social y la situación de las mujeres en una sociedad patriarcal: hablaba del sexo en contextos de dominación masculina, desigualdad económica, egoísmo de los hombres. “Constató categóricamente que la mayoría de las mujeres sufrían su sexualidad. Tienen más placer masturbándose que con su pareja. Menos de un tercio decía alcanzar el orgasmo con la penetración, y muchas sienten presión para tener relaciones por parte de la sociedad o de sus parejas”, escribe la terapeuta sexual Charline Vermont en el prefacio de la última edición, publicada en Francia en 2026.

Una muestra clara del clima de la época es que, cuando el informe llegó a las librerías, violar a la propia esposa era legal en la mayoría de los estados de EE UU y no constituía delito en España (ni en muchos países de Europa), donde los tribunales tardarían todavía dos décadas en reconocerlo y desprenderse de esa idea del “débito conyugal”.

Hite, que escapaba en su informe al paradigma de la heterosexualidad y evocaba todo tipo de relaciones sexuales, tuvo que defenderse de las acusaciones de misandria explicando que no veía “de qué modo la igualdad era peligrosa”. Años después, en un segundo informe dedicado a la sexualidad masculina, aseguraba que su intención era liberar a los hombres del peso de sus supuestas obligaciones sexuales. “Es difícil para un hombre criticar la idea de masculinidad porque, si lo hace, ya sea en el plano sexual o profesional, se arriesga a ser despreciado por otros hombres que dirán que no es un hombre de verdad”, decía en una entrevista en los ochenta. Poco después, se fue de Estados Unidos y renunció a su nacionalidad para obtener la alemana. Murió en 2020, a los 77 años.

Pese al éxito y el impacto de El Informe Hite, hoy sigue siendo difícil hacerse con un ejemplar en librerías. En España está descatalogado desde hace décadas, y la última edición rastreable data de los años ochenta. El 50º aniversario del informe está facilitando ciertas reediciones, como el caso de Francia; o en Estados Unidos, donde acaban de recuperar el estudio que publicó años después con encuestas sobre sexualidad masculina.

Shere Hite en una imagen de archivo. Owen Franken - Corbis (Getty Images)

A la educadora sexual Andrea Aguilar, autora del libro Mujer orgásmica, sin embargo, no le sorprende que haya desaparecido de las librerías. “Las cosas tienen sus momentos”, opina. “Este libro ya hizo su aporte. Por desgracia, no está suficientemente desfasado: debería estarlo mucho más. Ahora lo que tenemos que hacer es otra cosa”, defiende. Para Aguilar, la revolución que encarnaron Hite y las de su generación dando voz a las mujeres, poniendo el clítoris en el mapa y reivindicando que el placer femenino importaba, era “necesaria e imprescindible”, pero se construyó en buena medida imitando el modelo masculino: la descarga rápida, el orgasmo como meta. “Hemos reconquistado una parte, pero ahora nos queda conquistar el verdadero potencial del placer femenino. ¿Podemos ahora hacer la segunda revolución?”, propone.

Esa segunda revolución, dice, pasa por una sexualidad menos centrada en el rendimiento y también por volver a hacer lo que hizo Hite: preguntar. Medio siglo después, quedan territorios enteros del placer femenino sin apenas investigación científica (Aguilar cita la eyaculación femenina), y quizá haga falta una nueva encuesta a gran escala que retrate, como en 1976, lo que las mujeres sienten de verdad.

Por su parte, Sierra lamenta que “hemos cambiado el conocimiento mucho más rápido de lo que hemos cambiado la cultura” y, aunque el tiempo y los estudios han dado la razón a mucho de lo que adelantó Hite, “sigue existiendo y afectando la brecha orgásmica, es decir, de la diferencia en la frecuencia con la que hombres y mujeres alcanzan el orgasmo, especialmente en las relaciones heterosexuales”. “Culturalmente seguimos bastante centrados en la penetración y en una visión muy finalista del sexo”, sostien Sierra. Quizá esa sea la mejor explicación de por qué un libro que vendió 50 millones de ejemplares no se encuentra hoy en las librerías: su tesis ya no escandaliza, pero sus preguntas siguen resonando en la actualidad. “El gran legado de El Informe Hite”, concluye Sierra, “fue recordarnos que escuchar la experiencia de las mujeres no era una cuestión ideológica; era una forma de hacer mejor ciencia”.

World.title: “Era desagradable a la vista, pero pensamos que tenía posibilidades”: cómo un arquitecto español “tiró” una casa de Los Ángeles para resucitarla
World.content:
Ubicada al nordeste de la ciudad californiana, Casa Granada conserva la esencia de la arquitectura colonial española, pero también admite muebles ‘mid-century’, como sillas de los Eames, objetos de estética industrial y algunos toques ‘art nouveau’

Solemos pensar en el ejercicio de la arquitectura como un proceso perfectamente ordenado de adición de elementos y materiales. Sin embargo, en la casa Granada de Los Ángeles todo se hizo al revés. La obsesión de sus dueños fue retirar capas para recuperar el carácter de una construcción con más de un siglo de historia e insuflarle una vida completamente nueva a lo antiguo. Este rompecabezas arquitectónico ofrece una lección muy valiosa: identificar qué es lo que sobra en una casa puede ser una tarea mucho más gratificante y fructífera que centrarse en todo lo que le falta. Aquí sí, menos es más.

El baño mira hacia una 'bay window' que introduce la vegetación también en un espacio íntimo. Ignacio Espigares Enríquez

El arquitecto cántabro Juan Sáez Pedraja y su mujer, la música californiana Lexi Carr, estaban buscando casa cuando, casi por casualidad, llegaron a Highland Park, en el nordeste de Los Ángeles. El barrio tiene algo de remoto: el clima es distinto, más cálido y seco que en la costa, y su imagen tampoco tiene nada que ver con la típica postal angelina de playa, mansiones y grandes autopistas. A principios del siglo XX fue el hogar de una comunidad numerosa de arquitectos, obreros y artesanos que trabajaban en la construcción de los bellos bungalows Arts and Crafts de Pasadena, unas pocas millas hacia el este. Más cien años después, Highland Park mantiene esa esencia, con una escala urbana y un tejido residencial propios de otro tiempo. “Nos pareció un lugar muy interesante”, explica Sáez Pedraja. “Hay bastantes zonas peatonales con bares y restaurantes, galerías de arte y tiendas guays. Es hípster, pero tampoco demasiado”.

Los azulejos de las paredes de los baños proceden de una fábrica española. Ignacio Espigares Enríquez

Y entonces, se toparon con una pequeña casa escondida en la calle Granada. “Tiene una localización muy bonita, elevada, entre dos fondos de saco. La vimos y dijimos: ‘es esta”. Construida en 1920, por fuera responde al arquetipo de lo que por allí se conoce como Mission Revival, un estilo basado en la reinterpretación de la arquitectura de las misiones españolas en California que se volvió muy popular en Los Ángeles en las primeras décadas del siglo XX. Por dentro, la perspectiva no era tan romántica. “Habían cubierto las paredes y los techos con placas de yeso pintadas con gotelé de un color azul bastante feo, y en los suelos habían puesto un vinilo terrible”, nos cuenta el arquitecto. “Era una cosa un poco desagradable a la vista, pero pensamos que tenía posibilidades”.

Sáez Pedraja eligió unos mecanismos eléctricos de latón sin lacar que mantienen el aspecto artesano de la casa. Ignacio Espigares Enríquez

La pareja abordó la reforma como un “proyecto arqueológico” en el que, a golpe de martillo, iban demoliendo esa cáscara de gotelé para descubrir lo que había debajo. “Un edificio con historia te obliga a dialogar con él”, explica Sáez Pedraja. “Conforme íbamos retirando materiales añadidos, la casa nos daba pistas de lo que teníamos que hacer. Todas las decisiones acerca de qué se quedaba y qué no, las tomábamos sobre la marcha. Esa improvisación hace que las cosas estén vivas”. Este proceso orgánico espoleado por la curiosidad, más enfocado en rescatar la identidad propia de la casa que en crear una nueva, parece todo lo contrario de un proyecto de arquitectura. “No tenía un presupuesto cerrado. ¡Ni siquiera hice un solo dibujo! Para mí, los planos son como una autopsia: en cuanto los terminas y los entregas, ya sabes cómo va a terminar. A partir de ahí, se acaba lo divertido, y todo son permisos, presupuestos y problemas en la obra. Ya no puedes inventar”.

La estructura de madera de los techos se deja a la vista como un guiño al origen de la casa. Ignacio Espigares Enríquez

Mientras demolía, las posibles vidas de la casa se multiplicaban en la cabeza del arquitecto. El revoco de algunos muros interiores le indujo a pensar que quizá alguna vez habían sido exteriores, y que lo que hoy es su salón pudo haber sido antes un patio. En las paredes aparecieron ventanas que habían sido cegadas. Al abrirlas de nuevo, la casa resultó ser mucho más luminosa de lo que parecía en un principio, y los árboles frutales y el olmo chino del jardín se incorporaron al paisaje interior.

Cuando eliminó los falsos techos, se encontró con la estructura primitiva de vigas de abeto Douglas, una madera muy resistente, de un color rojizo precioso. También se retiraron revestimientos de vinilo y baldosas para sacar a la luz la tarima original. La sensación de caminar descalzo por un suelo de más de cien años es increíble. Cruje y huele. Toda la casa huele a madera. “Me alegro de que lo hayas notado. La dueña anterior era una señora que tenía muchísimos gatos, y cuando la compramos, apestaba”, dice Sáez Pedraja entre risas.

El dormitorio principal se abre hacia el jardín de la casa, que se incorpora al paisaje interior. Ignacio Espigares Enríquez

Por supuesto, no todo fueron buenas noticias. “Había mucho moho y muchas termitas”, recuerda el arquitecto. El suelo del salón estaba demasiado dañado, así que tuvo que reemplazarse. Utilizaron madera reciclada procedente de unas vigas antiguas, que cortaron y colocaron a 45 grados, atando visualmente los dos ejes perpendiculares que rigen el orden en planta. Esas imperfecciones y una ejecución descaradamente amateur refuerzan el alma artesanal de la casa. De hecho, no sólo la demolición, también la mayoría de los trabajos de construcción los realizó el arquitecto con sus propias manos y con un ayuda de un amigo músico en paro. “Todo esto lo hicimos en pleno confinamiento por la covid-19”, explica Sáez Pedraja. “Ni podía salir de gira, ni había conciertos. Él no tenía trabajo, pero sí herramientas”.

Otras decisiones de diseño, aunque más sutiles, también imprimen personalidad a la obra. Por ejemplo, el arquitecto reemplazó los mecanismos eléctricos por unos de latón sin lacar. “Quiero que mi casa envejezca, que tenga textura. No me gustan esos interruptores inteligentes de hoy en día en los que puedes regular mil cosas. Esa interfaz está bien para un teléfono, pero no para un interruptor. Yo prefiero sentir el tacto de la palanquita cuando enciendo una luz”.

Las plantas de interior conectan la casa con el clima y la vegetación exteriores. Ignacio Espigares Enríquez

Una vez la vivienda estaba recuperada, llegó el momento de habitarla. En línea con ese trabajo intuitivo de la reforma, la pareja entendió el interior como un lienzo en blanco receptivo a influencias superpuestas. El techo a dos aguas del salón, con el entramado de vigas y viguetas de madera a la vista, remite al carácter original de la construcción. “Cinco meses antes de comprarla visité la misión española de La Purísima Concepción en Lompoc, tres horas al norte de Los Ángeles. Es la que sale al final de Una batalla tras otra, de Paul Thomas Anderson. El otro día estaba viendo la película y me di cuenta de que seguramente aquella imagen, quizá de un modo inconsciente, me rondaba la cabeza cuando estaba trabajando en la casa”. Los alicatados de los baños proceden de una fábrica española. Pero hay algo más, algo que conecta la casa con la tradición mediterránea. ¿Qué es? “¡Las alicantinas!”, exclama Sáez Pedraja. “Compré estas persianas en España. En Estados Unidos no conciben la protección solar por fuera de la ventana. No lo entiendo, porque es mucho más lógico bloquear el sol antes de que incida en el vidrio, y no después, como les gusta aquí”.

En el comedor, se combinan las sillas DSX y la Plastic Armchair RE DAR diseñadas por Charles y Ray Eames en la década de 1950 con lámparas 'art nouveau'. Ignacio Espigares Enríquez

La casa Granada conserva la esencia de la arquitectura colonial española, pero también admite muebles mid-century californianos, como las sillas de los Eames del comedor, objetos de estética industrial y algunos toques art nouveau. Nada de lo que vemos es atrezo, sino los elementos cotidianos que construyen el hogar familiar. En el salón, suena el viejo piano Yamaha en el que Carr compone sus canciones, y lo preside la chimenea, forrada con un conjunto de baldosas de cerámica con bajorrelieves hechas a mano por Ernest A. Batchelder, un artista y destacado líder del movimiento Arts and Crafts local. Sobre la repisa, descansa una escultura de un pez verde (“Es el regalo de una amiga. Es de Mali, y huele muy bien. Huele a madera”) y una lámina del ilustrador franco-ruso Romain de Tirtoff, conocido como Erté , comprada en el Rose Bowl Flea Market de Pasadena. A su lado, en la ventana hay una vidriera con un gato. “Mi teoría es que se elaboró en Judson Studios , una empresa familiar de aquí, de Los Ángeles, que lleva haciendo vidrieras desde el siglo XIX, y que la puso ahí la anterior dueña”.

En la casa Granada, uno tiene la sensación de que el tiempo se detiene. “Yo creo que funciona porque no es un proyecto de arquitectura. No está pensada. Es pura intuición”, concluye el arquitecto. Y si luego algo no te gusta, siempre puedes deshacerte de ello a martillazos. De eso va esta casa, ¿no? “¡Claro! Quitar es mucho más barato que poner. Y más bonito.”

World.title: La guerra de las notas
World.content:
Jóvenes, Esperando a realizar las Pruebas de Acceso a la Universidad (PAU) en el Politécnico de Valencia, el pasado junio.

Texto en el que el autor aboga por ideas y saca conclusiones basadas en su interpretación de hechos y datos

La tradición dicta que un mejor o peor verano depende en gran parte del número de suspensos con el que tu hijo despidió el curso escolar en junio. Y ya no hablamos si le tocó repetir.

Cada final de trimestre, miles de familias españolas viven ese pequeño drama doméstico: se trata de valorar si el esfuerzo o la falta de éste ha tenido fiel correspondencia. Luego está lo que cada tutor plasma en el boletín de notas, claro está, si lo logramos entender.

La información sobre las calificaciones finales debería ser clara y comprensible, pero las nuevas leyes la han convertido en un jeroglífico pedagógico: Siglas como IN, SU, BI, NT y SB o códigos como PA, AD, MA y EX resultan familiares a muchos; ya cuando son mayores, en Bachillerato, empezamos a ver los tradicionales números, que recuerdan por fin a un lenguaje común. El legendario 0 o el deseado 10 son termómetros que auditan lo que cualquiera de nuestros chavales hizo durante el año escolar.

La evaluación escolar debería ser ese deseable puente entre escuela y familia, parte de una conversación pedagógica cercana, pero se ha transformado en un lenguaje paralelo que muchos no entienden. Y en ese desconcierto cotidiano se libra la guerra de las notas.

Cada nueva reforma escolar quiere cambiar la cultura evaluativa del sistema educativo español. Ahora más que nunca se habla de una evaluación continua, formativa y competencial, centrada en recorridos más que en resultados. Pero, erre que erre, el código que todos entendemos sigue siendo un número. Mi hijo y el del vecino serán siempre ese ocho o ese nueve que ha colocado a los jóvenes en una competición ya histórica.

Entre la teoría y la práctica se abre una brecha que explica buena parte de las confusiones actuales, que muchas veces desembocan en reclamaciones al final: el trabajo del profesor, puesto en duda.

Para las familias, el boletín es el único documento que reciben para saber cómo progresa su hijo o hija, pero el sistema les entrega un código que no siempre saben interpretar. ¿Qué diferencia real hay entre un “Bien” y un “Notable”? ¿Cómo es posible que una competencia esté en “Adecuado” pero la materia aparezca suspensa? ¿Qué significa realmente una lista de criterios de evaluación no superados anotados en una observación de un documento digital? Dicho de otra manera: ¿Qué les contamos a las familias sobre sus hijos y qué necesitan saber realmente?

La normativa pudiera parecer clara en su estructura, pero no en su traducción social. La escuela lleva años hablando un idioma técnico que confunde hasta a los docentes, refugiados en tecnicismos ante el temor a represalias. Imaginemos la situación de las familias, que además no tienen un asistente que les traduzca todo este lenguaje, más allá de lo que la IA, con sus errores, ofrece como solución.

Mientras, el profesorado vive esta guerra desde la trinchera, pidiendo hace años aclarar y unificar esta neolengua. Se exige diseñar instrumentos, matrices, rúbricas, indicadores de logro o evidencias. Así, un largo etcétera: son las herramientas para medir lo que el estudiante va aprendiendo. El resultado es que nos enfrentamos a tres tensiones simultáneas: la presión social por calificar, la obligación normativa de evaluar según nuevos estándares y la necesidad imperiosa de comunicar con claridad (obligación de la administración). El resultado: vivimos en un sistema donde el profesorado dedica excesivo tiempo a justificar la calificación final de sus estudiantes.

Las paradojas son evidentes. La evaluación debe ser objetiva, válida y fiable, pero la evaluación competencial introduce inevitablemente un alto componente interpretativo. La guerra de las notas es, en realidad, la guerra entre dos modelos que conviven enfrentados: el modelo tradicional, basado en la calificación numérica y la aparente objetividad, y el modelo competencial, basado en el desempeño y la interpretación profesional, al que no logramos acostumbrarnos.

La evaluación es también un fenómeno cultural. Durante décadas, las notas han sido el principal mecanismo de reconocimiento social del éxito escolar. Cambiar ese paradigma exige tiempo, formación y una narrativa compartida que no existe. Las familias quieren claridad. El profesorado, coherencia. La administración, rigor. El alumnado quiere saber si lo está haciendo bien. Todos hablan lenguajes distintos.

La guerra de las notas no se resolverá con más tablas que rellenar. Se resolverá cuando el sistema educativo asuma tres cambios profundos: el primero, la creación de un lenguaje común: necesitamos una gramática comprensible para todos, definitiva y alejada de modismos. Hay que explicar qué significa un resultado y cómo se interpreta. El segundo es una formación masiva y unificada en evaluación. La evaluación competencial exige una claridad técnica que dé seguridad al profesorado. El tercero es un modelo de comunicación transparente con las familias. Los boletines deben ser comprensibles, contextualizados y acompañados de información accesible.

La evaluación es el corazón del sistema educativo. De ella dependen la equidad, la calidad y la confianza social. Hoy, ese corazón late en un idioma ininteligible, y eso genera una desconfianza que se plasma en reclamaciones. Pero estamos ante un conflicto evitable. La guerra de las notas puede convertirse en paz si logramos que la evaluación deje de ser un código y vuelva a ser lo que siempre debió ser: una conversación honesta sobre el aprendizaje.

World.title: Ajax, ING and Ace & Tate hit by data breach
World.content:
