World.title: Canadian Estonian family still thriving 30 years after return to homeland
World.content:
The Viinalass family recently celebrated 30 years in Estonia, reflecting on how a temporary move to their homeland became permanent, coming full circle after generations.

The family marked the milestone with a gathering of about 150 relatives and friends, who shared memories from their early years after moving from Canada.

"Our mom was in charge of the Facebook event," recalled Joshua James Viinalass, a real estate broker with Arco Vara.

"She accidentally sent the invite to everyone," added his brother, musician Daniel Levi. "And everyone responded that they're coming."

Like in many diaspora Estonian families, the Viinalass brothers' grandfather was a World War II-era refugee, who first fled to Germany in 1944 before reaching and later naturalizing as a citizen in Canada.

Their father, Linden Viinalass, was born and raised in Canada, where his children were also born and spent the first few years of their lives. After their grandfather's death in the 1990s, however, their father came across an ad in a Canadian Estonian diaspora newspaper seeking English teachers in Estonia.

"He immediately knew that [opportunity] was meant for him — like it spoke to him almost supernaturally," Daniel Levi said.

The plan was simple: move to Estonia for a year and then return to Canada. Thirty years later, the family is still here and thriving.

Adjusting as kids

Joshua James and Daniel Levi were just 3 and 8 years old when their family moved to Tartu, and some of their earliest memories are of life in and around the Soviet-era prefab apartment buildings in Annelinn.

Viinalass family photos. Source: Viinalass family/ERR

Joshua James said he picked up Estonian simply playing with other kids on the playground and in kindergarten.

Daniel Levi recalled his father giving a neighbor's child a soccer ball, which prompted an unexpected gift to the Viinalass family in turn.

"The family was so touched that they gifted us a drinking horn brought all the way from Georgia in return," he said, adding that the horn is still proudly displayed at their parents' home.

The musician acknowledged that the move from Canada to Estonia took some getting used to for all of them, but added that the younger you are, the easier it can be to adjust.

"Speaking of adjusting, just today I was talking to someone about what our favorite parts of kindergarten had been," said Joshua James. "I remember I couldn't understand a word at first, but when meals were served, that was the best part of the day."

Both brothers praised Estonian food, agreeing that one of their favorite Estonian dishes is still hakklihakaste — a simple creamed ground meat often served with potatoes and popular both in Estonia and the diaspora.

Years after a previous appearance on ETV's "Ringvaade," however, Daniel Levi admitted he still can't bring himself to eat sült, or meat aspic.

Brothers Daniel Levi Viinalass and James Joshua Viinalass. August 2026. Source: ERR

'Three men sitting in a sauna'

Asked whether Estonia lives up to its digital image, the Viiinalass brothers pointed out that the contrast is evident when they talk to friends in the U.S. who still have to deposit physical paychecks in person at the bank, or grapple with filing tax returns that in Estonia take literally just a few clicks to do.

They also agreed Estonians seem to be warming up to things like hugging, although the perception that Estonians are typically reserved and need their personal space persists.

"Estonians like their fresh air and pure nature, and I think that sense of personal space goes beyond just that question of hugging," said Daniel Levi.

"I think it's very healthy," Joshua James countered, prompting his brother to quip that it's clear he was raised in Estonia. "That little bit of personal space is really welcome sometimes."

The real estate broker described his post-workout sauna at the gym earlier that day, calling it a perfectly Estonian example.

"Three men sitting in a sauna: no one says a word, no one makes eye contact, no one says 'Tere,' nothing," Joshua James said. "No, when I handed the water bucket over to one of the other guys in the sauna, he said, 'Aitäh.'"

World.title: Iraq oil exports drop 75% amid Hormuz closure
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Oil Minister Hayan Abdul-Ghani announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, that the nation’s crude oil exports have plummeted by 75% due to the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and regional military escalations. The severe drop in oil revenues has triggered a liquidity squeeze across the federal government, causing widespread delays in state employee salary disbursements.

Speaking at a press conference in Baghdad, Abdul-Ghani revealed that Iraq is currently exporting only a quarter of its pre-war volumes, which stood at approximately 3.5 million barrels per day (bpd) prior to the outbreak of regional hostilities on February 28. He noted that while Baghdad has engaged in diplomatic talks with Iran to permit the passage of Iraqi oil shipments through the Gulf, no operational agreement has been activated.

Key financial and operational highlights

Export Collapse: Iraq’s crude exports have fallen to ~25% of pre-war capacity, cutting off the primary source of state revenue.

Fiscal Pressure & Salary Delays: Reduced export volumes and below-budget sale prices have caused acute liquidity shortages, delaying public sector payrolls.

Corporate Damage Compensation: Domestic Attacks: Baghdad has agreed to compensate foreign energy companies for damages resulting from attacks originating inside Iraqi territory. External Strikes: The government declared itself legally exempt from compensating firms for damages caused by foreign strikes or broader military actions beyond state control.

Alternative Export Bypasses: Baghdad is fast-tracking pipeline infrastructure projects bypassing the Persian Gulf, including routes south toward Turkey’s Ceyhan port, Syria’s Baniyas terminal, and Jordan’s Aqaba port.

To maintain minimal cash flows, Iraq is currently forced to sell its crude at deep price concessions below the baseline benchmark set in the national budget, compounding treasury deficits.

In response to the prolonged maritime chokehold in the Strait of Hormuz, the Ministry of Oil is accelerating infrastructure development along overland export routes.

Priority has been placed on expanding and constructing pipeline corridors connecting southern production hubs to the Mediterranean via Syria and Turkey, alongside long-term transit planning toward the Red Sea via Jordan.

World.title: Iraq activates Kirkuk oil field development contract with BP
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Saturday, August 8, 2026, the official activation of its Kirkuk oilfield development contract with British energy giant BP. The project aims to elevate crude oil production from its current capacity of 320,000 barrels per day (bpd) to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Ministry of Oil Spokesperson Salim Al-Rikabi stated that the contract—initially signed in September 2025—focuses on expanding crude extraction while capturing associated natural gas to eliminate routine flaring and feed domestic power generation infrastructure.

Key operational targets & metrics

Crude Oil Output: Increasing current production from 320,000 bpd to a peak target of 420,000 bpd.

Associated Gas Capture: Raising associated gas processing from 255 million standard cubic feet per day (scf/d) to a peak capacity of 400 million scf/d.

Facility Modernization: Upgrading and expanding infrastructure across North Oil Company fields and North Gas Company processing plants.

Power & Social Infrastructure: Constructing a dedicated 400-megawatt (MW) power plant, expanding local employment, funding community development initiatives, and upskilling North Oil and North Gas workforces.

Environmental Impact: Phasing out continuous gas flaring to redirect captured methane directly into national electricity generation.

The activation of the Kirkuk project represents a major component of Iraq’s broader energy strategy to achieve natural gas self-sufficiency and reduce reliance on imported fuel.

By upgrading processing facilities managed by the North Gas Company and constructing a dedicated 400 MW power generation facility, the initiative directly addresses regional electricity shortages while reducing environmental emissions.

The partnership also reinforces BP’s operational footprint in northern Iraq, complementing its long-standing management of the Southern Rumaila field and bolstering state-led efforts to modernize national energy infrastructure.

World.title: India’s Reliance pays record $25 million freight cost for Iraqi crude amid Hormuz crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — India’s Reliance Industries (RELI.NS), operator of the world’s largest refining complex in Gujarat, paid an unprecedented record charter fee of $23 million to $25 million for a Very Large Crude Carrier (VLCC) to transport 2 million barrels of Basrah crude from Iraq, according to shipping sources cited by Reuters on Friday, August 7, 2026.

The extreme freight surge—marking a jump from a pre-war average of $2 million to 12 times the baseline global freight rate—highlights severe shipping chokepoints in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Daily vessel transits through the strategic waterway have plummeted from a pre-war average of 125–140 ships to a fraction of normal capacity as shipowners avoid military risks.

Key financial & logistics metrics

Soaring Freight Rates: Reliance chartered the VLCC from South Korea’s Sinokor at 1,200 points on the Worldscale freight index—12 times the reference benchmark—up from pre-war levels of 0.8 to 0.9 times ($2 million total).

Deep SOMO Discounts: To offset soaring shipping costs and attract buyers into the Gulf, the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) offered steep discounts of $25 to $30 per barrel below Dubai regional benchmarks.

Net Margin Offset: Despite the $25 million freight tag, energy analysts estimate Reliance will still save millions on the overall transaction due to Iraq’s heavy crude price reductions.

Limited Carrier Pool: Sinokor remains one of the few international maritime operators willing to navigate the Strait of Hormuz to load cargo at Iraq’s Basra Oil Terminal.

While Asian refiners—particularly across India and China—are actively seeking chartered tankers to capture Iraq’s discounted crude allocations, shipowner reluctance continues to limit available tonnage entering the Gulf.

By offering deep price concessions, Iraq’s oil marketing arm is successfully maintaining crude flow off the Basra coast despite soaring war-risk insurance premiums and maritime transport bottlenecks.

World.title: Kata’ib Sayyid Al Shuhada clarifies delay in retaliatory strikes against U.S.-Saudi targets
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Abu Ala al-Walai, Secretary-General of Kata’ib Sayyid al-Shuhada, commented on Saturday, August 8, 2026, regarding the decision by the “Islamic Resistance in Iraq” to pause planned military responses to recent joint U.S.-Saudi strikes.

Speaking via a statement on social media platform X, al-Walai confirmed that the delay was granted at the direct request of Coordination Framework leaders, led by Badr Organization chief Hadi al-Amiri, alongside several independent political figures. However, the paramilitary commander emphasized that options for retaliation—including the reassessment of its timing, scale, and nature—remain fully on the table. He urged state officials to utilize this temporary window to secure Iraq’s rights through diplomatic and legal channels.

Key developments in the escalation pause

The Deferred Response: The Islamic Resistance in Iraq announced on Friday, August 7, the postponement of retaliatory operations originally scheduled for the 23rd of Safar targeting Saudi Arabia and U.S. military bases.

Al-Amiri’s Appeal: Badr Organization leader Hadi al-Amiri issued an urgent video address early Friday urging armed factions to delay military action following American-Saudi strikes on Iraqi territory, prioritizing national stability while pursuing accountability for casualties via diplomatic means.

High Security Readiness: The political appeal followed a volatile night across Baghdad and multiple governorates, prompting high-level security alerts and military deployments across the capital.

Command Structure On Site: In response to directives from Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi to elevate combat readiness, senior commanders from Baghdad Operations Command were deployed on the ground to enforce military discipline and secure vital sectors.

The brief pause in military operations provides a critical window for Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s administration to manage state security, navigate delicate diplomatic channels with Washington and Riyadh, and prevent further regional escalation.

World.title: Iraq fish deaths: 7 alarming signs of a deepening water and pollution crisis
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Recurring Iraq fish deaths are becoming an increasingly serious environmental and economic warning, with the Green Iraq Observatory describing the phenomenon as an annual pattern that reflects the accumulation of two interconnected crises: worsening water scarcity and persistent pollution.

Rather than representing isolated incidents caused by temporary changes in river conditions, the repeated deaths of large numbers of fish across Iraq’s rivers, canals and marshlands suggest that the country’s aquatic ecosystems are coming under sustained pressure from declining water flows, untreated wastewater, industrial pollution and weaknesses in water management.

The latest incidents, recorded in April and August 2026, have once again raised concerns about the condition of Iraq’s freshwater resources and the government’s ability to protect them. According to the observatory, more than 1,000 tonnes of fish died in the Tigris and Diyala rivers during April, with particularly heavy losses reported in Wasit province, while a separate incident occurred earlier this month in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan.

Although the two incidents were associated with different immediate circumstances, they demonstrate how vulnerable Iraq’s aquatic ecosystems have become when declining water levels interact with pollution and inadequate environmental controls.

Iraq fish deaths are becoming an annual warning sign

The Green Iraq Observatory argues that the recurrence of mass fish deaths should no longer be treated as a series of unrelated environmental emergencies. According to its assessment, similar incidents have occurred repeatedly across different parts of Iraq over the past several years, yet the underlying causes have not been addressed with sufficient consistency to prevent them from returning.

This pattern is particularly concerning because rivers and wetlands are not only ecological assets; they also support fisheries, agriculture and the livelihoods of communities that depend directly on healthy waterways.

The observatory said the April incident involved more than 1,000 tonnes of dead fish in the Tigris and Diyala rivers, with the largest losses concentrated in Wasit. It attributed the event to severe contamination caused by untreated sewage and industrial waste, while also pointing to increased water releases from Hamrin Dam that reportedly moved accumulated pollutants downstream toward the Tigris.

The organization further said that more than 20 people experienced poisoning or skin-related injuries and were taken to hospital, illustrating how deterioration in water quality can potentially extend beyond damage to aquatic life and become a broader public-health concern.

A second incident was reported at the beginning of August in the Al-Amshan Canal in Maysan. According to the observatory, the agriculture and water committee of the Maysan Provincial Council attributed the fish deaths to a sharp decline in the water releases allocated to the canal.

This episode is significant because it demonstrates that pollution is not necessarily the only immediate trigger for fish mortality; inadequate water flows can also create conditions in which fish become increasingly vulnerable to high temperatures, reduced oxygen levels and the concentration of pollutants already present in the water.

Water scarcity Is only part of the problem

Iraq’s water crisis is frequently discussed in terms of declining river flows, prolonged drought and reductions in water arriving from upstream countries. Those factors are undoubtedly important, but the recent fish deaths suggest that the country’s environmental problems cannot be explained simply by saying that Iraq does not have enough water. The quality, distribution and management of the water available can be just as important as its overall volume.

The Green Iraq Observatory highlighted this distinction by noting that the country’s total water storage had reportedly risen to around 34 billion cubic meters at the time of the latest incident.

From the organization’s perspective, the fact that fish mortality continued despite an increase in total reserves indicates that administrative decisions concerning water distribution may be contributing to the problem alongside genuine resource scarcity.

This does not mean that Iraq’s wider water shortage is unimportant. On the contrary, prolonged drought and declining inflows can weaken the natural ability of rivers and wetlands to dilute pollutants and maintain ecological balance. However, when available water is distributed unevenly or when polluted water is allowed to enter already stressed waterways, the consequences can become significantly more severe.

In other words, the crisis is not simply about how much water Iraq has, but also about where the water goes, what quality it has and how effectively it is managed.

Pollution can turn a water shortage into an ecological emergency

Untreated sewage and industrial waste are among the most serious threats facing Iraq’s waterways because they can fundamentally alter the chemical and biological conditions required for aquatic life. When large quantities of organic material enter a river or canal, microorganisms consume oxygen while breaking that material down, potentially reducing dissolved oxygen to levels that fish and other aquatic organisms cannot tolerate.

The situation can become even more complicated when water temperatures rise or when algae proliferate excessively. Some forms of harmful algae can contribute to oxygen depletion, particularly when large quantities of organic matter subsequently decompose.

At the same time, reduced water flows can prevent pollutants from being dispersed naturally, leaving them concentrated in particular sections of a river, canal or wetland.

This combination of factors helps explain why pollution and water scarcity should not be treated as completely separate problems. A waterway with strong flows may have a greater capacity to dilute certain pollutants, whereas a shallow and poorly circulated waterway can become significantly more vulnerable to contamination.

Consequently, environmental protection requires both adequate water releases and strict control over what is discharged into the country’s rivers.

Iraq has experienced similar fish mortality events for years

The latest incidents are not without precedent. The Green Iraq Observatory cited a long record of mass fish mortality events in Iraq, including a major incident in the Euphrates in Babylon in 2018, when tens of thousands of tonnes of fish were reportedly affected.

This was followed by the death of millions of fish at the Hindiya Barrage and another major incident in Al-Dalm Marsh in Diwaniyah in 2020.

Further incidents were reported in the Al-Ezz River in Maysan in 2023, while extensive fish deaths occurred in Ibn Najm Marsh in Najaf last year. Particularly worrying is the recurrence of fish mortality in the Maysan area where a similar incident had already been recorded, because repeated events in the same geographic location can indicate that the environmental conditions responsible for the original problem have not been adequately corrected.

The observatory argues that the repeated nature of these incidents is difficult to reconcile with a system that relies primarily on temporary investigative committees after environmental damage has already occurred. Investigations can establish causes and responsibility, but they cannot substitute for permanent monitoring mechanisms capable of identifying dangerous changes in water quality before they result in large-scale ecological losses.

Iraq’s Marshlands face particular risks

The Iraqi marshlands are especially sensitive to changes in water availability and quality because their ecological health depends on a delicate relationship between water flows, seasonal conditions and the surrounding environment. These wetlands provide habitat for fish and birds while supporting communities whose economic and cultural lives have developed around them over generations.

When water levels fall sharply, sections of the marshes can become isolated or excessively shallow, increasing temperatures and reducing oxygen circulation. If polluted water enters these already stressed environments, the damage can become significantly more difficult to reverse.

Protecting Iraq’s marshlands therefore requires a long-term approach that connects water policy with environmental policy. Maintaining adequate ecological flows, reducing pollution and establishing continuous monitoring systems would be far more effective than treating each fish mortality event as an isolated emergency.

What Iraq can do to prevent future fish deaths

The Green Iraq Observatory has called for several measures aimed at addressing the structural causes behind recurring fish mortality. Among its recommendations is the establishment of fair and sustainable water allocations for provinces and marshlands, rather than relying on short-term decisions that may leave some waterways dangerously depleted.

The observatory has also called for stronger environmental oversight of wastewater treatment facilities and industrial establishments located near rivers. Effective enforcement would require more than regulations on paper; authorities would need regular inspections, reliable water-quality testing and meaningful consequences for facilities that discharge untreated or inadequately treated waste.

Another important proposal is the creation of an early-warning system that monitors dissolved oxygen and pollution levels. Such a system could bring together government agencies, universities and civil-society organizations, allowing scientific data to be collected continuously and shared quickly when dangerous changes are detected.

Finally, rapid compensation for fish farmers affected by major environmental incidents could provide essential economic relief while investigations determine responsibility and long-term solutions.

No. Water scarcity is an important contributing factor, but pollution and poor water management can also play major roles. Even when overall water reserves increase, individual rivers, canals or marshes may experience insufficient flows or deteriorating water quality.

World.title: US Fed sends $500 million cash shipment to Iraq amid financial pressures
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The United States Federal Reserve has sent a new $500 million cash cargo to the Central Bank of Iraq, providing additional dollar liquidity as Baghdad grapples with rising financial pressures and disruptions to its oil-dependent economy.

The shipment was announced by Iraq’s national news agency, citing an official source who claimed the dollars will be used for permitted overseas transfers and transactions involving Iraqi citizens.

Further supplies are planned each month, with a government official estimating annual cash delivery of $8 billion to $10 billion.

These cash payments are part of Iraq’s peculiar financial relationship with the United States.

Proceeds from Iraqi oil exports are mostly placed in an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, with Baghdad obtaining dollars via permitted transfers and cash shipments administered by the Central Bank of Iraq.

The new supply comes at a critical moment for Iraq’s budget.

The disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has increased pressure on a nation that relies significantly on oil exports to support government expenditures and get foreign currency.

Iraq’s enormous public-sector pay bill contributes to this vulnerability.

Millions of Iraqis rely directly or indirectly on government wages, pensions, and social benefits; therefore, stable oil income and liquidity are crucial to the national budget.

Baghdad has lately expressed increased worries about its capacity to fulfill expenditure obligations if oil earnings continue low, strengthening long-standing demands for Iraq to diversify government income and lessen its reliance on petroleum exports.

The most recent dollar cargo should offer further liquidity to Iraq’s banking system, but it also shows the country’s vulnerability to both oil-market shocks and its financial ties with Washington at a time of rising regional tensions.

World.title: Lise Klaveness, the Norwegian thorn in Infantino’s side
World.content:
Oslo – A rare woman in the top echelons of football, the head of Norway’s federation Lise Klaveness has been a thorn in FIFA’s side for years.

Now, some would gladly see her take over the leadership of football’s international governing body from Gianni Infantino.

The 45-year-old lawyer and former footballer who played 73 matches for Norway has been highly vocal about international football’s woes under Infantino.

The Swiss-Italian has been mired in controversy since his plan to open FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors was swiftly rejected last week.

On Friday she called for him to resign.

When he was elected FIFA president in 2016, “he was a candidate who had been elected on a reform programme focused on good governance,” she told AFP.

“Then things quickly deteriorated: from keeping a distance, we moved to giving up, and even backtracking, all against a backdrop of a lack of independence from heads of state and other influential figures, particularly from World Cup host countries,” she said.

She fired her first salvo at Infantino in 2022, just after she was appointed head of the Norwegian federation, about the conditions under which the World Cup was awarded to Qatar.

From Doha, she publicly lamented that “human rights, equality, democracy, the core interests of football, were not in the starting 11”.

The following year, Norway refused to back Infantino in his re-election bid, signalling its dissatisfaction with his leadership.

Klaveness “was in a way the first standard-bearer for much of this criticism that many others now share when it comes to the way Infantino runs FIFA,” said Mina Finsted Berg, a sports commentator for Norwegian channel TV2.

She “is very committed to ensuring that rules and decisions are respected,” she added.

– Trump, Balogun and investors –

The reasons for her outrage against Infantino have piled up in recent months: FIFA’s decision to award a “Peace Prize” to US President Donald Trump, with whom Infantino has a conspicuously close relationship; the lifting of the suspension of US player Folarin Balogun at the 2026 World Cup following an intervention by Trump; and the aborted plan to open FIFA to private investors.

The Norwegian federation has decided to bring all three issues before the Ethics Committee of the world football governing body.

Klaveness’s voice carries all the more weight after Norway, long absent from major international tournaments, enjoyed a strong run in this year’s World Cup before being knocked out in the quarter-finals by England.

Internationally, commentators have praised her “strong moral compass” and consider her a serious candidate to replace Infantino if he were to step down.

He is standing for re-election for a fourth and final term next March and is currently the only declared candidate.

“She was the only one who always took a clear stand and did not go along with the mainstream. And at FIFA, the time is right for a woman to take the lead,” former FIFA head Sepp Blatter — himself disgraced after a corruption scandal — wrote on social network X.

– Ballot box obstacles –

Klaveness herself has insisted that the crisis in world football should not be reduced to a simple “Game of Thrones” power struggle and has instead called for a renewed focus on good governance.

“For us, it has never been a personal issue against Gianni Infantino,” she told AFP. “The problems go beyond the person of the president.”

And while she “has registered” that her name is being tossed around as a possible successor, she brushed aside questions about whether she was a candidate: “We’re not there yet.”

Many obstacles remain.

“In addition to being seen as extremely radical in many places, especially outside Europe, she is a woman. That is also likely to count against her in many regions of the world,” Mina Finsted Berg said.

Even within Europe’s governing body UEFA, which one could presume would be most favourable to her, Klaveness failed to win election to the Executive Committee in 2023.

She only joined in 2025, when she was the sole candidate for the seat reserved for women.

“If she already has such a hard time getting elected in Europe, how could she convince Africans and South Americans?” asked Erik Thorstvedt, a former goalkeeper for the Norwegian national team turned commentator.

World.title: Clinton compares Trump’s White House to former Iraqi dictator Saddam’s palaces
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has compared President Donald Trump’s White House renovations to former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein’s palaces, remembering her own travels to Baghdad after his ouster.

Clinton, speaking on journalist Kara Swisher’s podcast, compared Trump’s White House decor to meetings she attended in Saddam Hussein’s former palaces while serving as a US senator.

“They were quite reminiscent of what we are seeing in our own White House,” she said.

Her remarks come amid wider criticism of Trump’s renovations and architectural decisions, such as heavy gold décor within the Oval Office, plans for a new White House ballroom, and a projected triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

Clinton called the improvements “tacky” and suggested that the president was focusing too much on cosmetic initiatives when the US confronts substantial foreign policy, economic, and technological issues.

She also criticized the process around Trump’s planned ballroom, stating that she was not opposed to the White House having such a facility but was concerned about the architecture and how the project had been handled.

Given Clinton’s past with Iraq, the connection to Saddam was especially relevant.

She was a member of the United States Senate during the 2003 war that deposed Saddam Hussein and subsequently became Secretary of State under President Barack Obama.

During his reign, Saddam was noted for building multiple extravagant presidential palaces around Iraq, many with elaborate interiors and significant use of marble, chandeliers, and gold-colored décor, despite the country’s international sanctions and economic difficulty.

Trump has defended his White House restoration plans, which are part of a larger push to renovate and enhance Washington’s important federal buildings and sites.

Clinton’s parallel brings Iraq and one of Saddam’s most recognizable emblems into the increasingly heated political argument over Trump’s White House moves.

World.title: ‘Gangstran Te Vaar’: Punjab Police acts against over 58,000 criminals in 200-day crackdown
World.content:
Punjab Policeâs flagship anti-gangster campaign âGangstran Te Vaarâ has completed 200 days, with the force claiming a major crackdown on organised crime networks across the state.

During the campaign, police conducted 1,09,087 raids, arrested 1,532 proclaimed offenders and initiated action against 58,212 criminals and their associates, according to official sources.

Crackdown targets entire organised crime ecosystem

Launched under the Bhagwant Mann government, the intelligence-driven campaign has focused not only on gangsters but also on their associates, financial networks, weapons supply, logistics and overseas handlers.

Police said preventive action was taken against 28,201 people, while another 18,514 were verified and released.

Overall, the campaign covered 1,04,927 persons, including gangsters, their associates and wanted criminals.

DGP Gaurav Yadav said the operation had evolved into a multi-dimensional campaign aimed at dismantling the ecosystem supporting organised crime.

âOur strategy goes beyond arrests to dismantling the ecosystem that enables organised crime by targeting associates, finances, logistics, communication channels and overseas linkages,â Yadav said.





Weapons, drugs and criminal infrastructure seized

The campaign also targeted the firepower and financial networks of organised gangs. Punjab Police recovered 990 illegal firearms, 242 sharp-edged weapons, 2,739 rounds of ammunition, 315 magazines, 2.5 kg of explosives and 15 hand grenades.

In its action against the crime-drug nexus, police seized 774.38 kg of heroin, 480.23 kg of opium, 7,266.26 kg of poppy husk and more than 26.91 lakh intoxicant tablets.

Authorities also seized Rs 1.73 crore in drug money, Rs 1.80 crore in cash and 413.85 grams of gold.

Overseas gangsters brought back

The Anti-Gangster Task Force (AGTF) also pursued fugitives operating from abroad. Police highlighted the deportation of gangster Bhuvnesh Chopra alias Ashish Chopra from Central Asia and Jobanjit Singh alias Joban Billa from Jakarta, Indonesia.

World.title: 'Dard, data, daulat': Rahul Gandhi targets Centre over unemployment at ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress leader

on Saturday described Indiaâs youth as the countryâs biggest strength, but said a lack of jobs, expensive education, paper leaks, poor access to credit and the growing use of AI were holding them back.

Speaking at the âChhatron Ki Goonjâ programme at KP Ground in Prayagraj, Rahul told the gathering, âYou are power and pride of India; when I say this, I talk about every Indian citizen.â He said he wanted to speak about âdard (pain), data, and daulat (wealth)â, framing his address around the problems facing young Indians and the economic resources he believes should belong to them.

Rahul said Indiaâs nearly 40 crore young people were its âgreatest strengthâ, adding that while there was much discussion about America, China and Russia, âIndiaâs youth [are] unparalleled.â

He argued that the country's future would depend on the potential of its young population and the data they generate.

He said artificial intelligence was also built on peopleâs data and argued that this data should be treated as an asset belonging to Indians. Rahul criticised the growing use of AI in discussions about employment, saying technological changes could further threaten jobs unless young people benefited from the economy being built around their data.





Rahul also spoke about his connection to Prayagraj, describing the city as his familyâs home and recalling its past as an important educational centre. He said Allahabad University had once been among the country's best universities.

Rahul said young Indians were being trapped in a âchakravyuhâ, with education becoming increasingly expensive while degrees often failed to translate into jobs.

âToday, education certificates have no meaning in India because they cannot give you job,â he said, arguing that students could spend years and large amounts of money on education without finding meaningful employment.

Rahul said the problems extended across several routes into the workforce. âAll doors of employment are closed in India,â he said, pointing to a decline in manufacturing, difficulties in securing loans, government-exam paper leaks and AI-driven job losses.

âDecline in manufacturing, hard-to-come-by loans, paper leaks, AI replacing jobs â all this is hurting India's youth,â Rahul said.

He blamed demonetisation and GST for hurting small industries, alleged that banks were failing to provide adequate credit to small and medium businesses, and criticised the privatisation of public-sector companies.

He also argued that AI could further reduce corporate employment while young Indians were increasingly pushed towards gig work.

Rahul framed these problems as part of what he called the broader âsystemâ, arguing that economic and political power had become concentrated among a small number of people. He linked this to his criticism of large corporations, the government and the RSS, alleging that they exercised disproportionate influence over India's institutions.

World.title: Bihar should withdraw alcohol ban as it failed to curb crimes against women: Report
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Bihar should withdraw its prohibition on alcohol as the ban has failed to reduce crimes against women and has been accompanied by a rise in illicit liquor and alternative intoxicants, according to a research paper by economic think tank National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER).

The paper, titled âMacro Perspective of Bihar's Development Achievements, Unfinished Agenda, and the Way Forwardâ, also said restoring liquor excise duty to pre-ban levels could increase the state's own revenues by 14-15 per cent while reducing expenditure on enforcement and anti-smuggling operations.

Prepared by a team of economists led by Ratna Sahay and presented at the India Policy Forum, the paper examined the economic and social impact of Bihar's prohibition, introduced in April 2016.

Ban failed to reduce crimes against women, says paper

The paper said the primary reasons for introducing prohibition were the belief that alcohol consumption contributed significantly to domestic violence and that households would redirect money previously spent on alcohol towards more productive uses.

Women's groups and activists had also strongly backed the ban, arguing that prohibition would reduce alcohol-related abuse.

However, the NCAER researchers said available data now allows an assessment of whether those objectives were achieved.





âWe now have sufficient data and information to assess if the ban was effective. Reported crimes against women in Bihar have not declined following the introduction of prohibition. Instead, total reported crimes against women increased over the post-2016 period,â the paper said.

According to the study, the available evidence does not show a broad-based reduction in crimes against women after prohibition. Instead, it said the ban coincided with concerns over the expansion of illicit liquor networks, enforcement difficulties and corruption.

The paper also pointed to increased use of alternative intoxicants, including illicit drugs.

âIn tandem, there was a significant rise in illegal liquor trade leading to higher alcohol consumption, increased crime and corruption, and an increase in the use of alternative additive substances, such as illicit drugs,â it said.

Prohibition has also hit state revenues

The NCAER paper said Bihar suffered significant fiscal consequences after the ban. Before prohibition, excise duty on alcohol accounted for about 14 per cent of the state's own revenues in the three years preceding the ban.

At the same time, the government incurred higher expenditure on monitoring, enforcement and anti-smuggling operations, which the paper said added to fiscal pressures.

The researchers argued that reinstating liquor excise duty at historical levels could help restore the contribution of the tax to around 14 per cent of state revenues.

The paper concluded that the prohibition had not achieved its intended objectives and had instead coincided with higher reported crimes against women, loss of state revenue and increased enforcement expenditure.

Education, health and jobs among Bihar's priorities

Beyond prohibition, the paper identified six interconnected areas that it said should form the core of Bihar's development strategy: education, health, governance and law and order, flood mitigation, private-sector development and women's empowerment.

It said reforms in these areas were necessary to improve productivity, accelerate structural transformation and create better-quality jobs for Bihar's young population.

The study also examined the state's public debt and fiscal sustainability, and assessed the financing required for different reform scenarios. It called for a combination of stronger own-revenue mobilisation, more efficient public spending, additional central government support and, where necessary, further borrowing.

World.title: Pests, mould, live insects: FSSAI suspends license of two food units
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has suspended the licences of two food manufacturers in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra after inspections uncovered serious food safety violations, including live insects in pistachios, rodent droppings, fungal growth, unhygienic processing conditions and ineffective pest control.

The action was taken against VKC Nuts Private Limited (Uttar Pradesh) and Chheda Specialities Foods Pvt Ltd (Maharashtra), with FSSAI saying the deficiencies posed a potential risk to public health.

At VKC Nuts, inspectors found live insects in stored pistachios, heavy black mould on storage walls and ceilings, rodent droppings across the premises, rusted machinery, damaged flooring, houseflies on food products and a live lizard near open crates of figs.

They also found a food handler sorting figs with a bandaged hand and another handling dry fruits without prescribed corrective spectacles. The unit scored 38% in FSSAI's compliance assessment, following which its licence was partially suspended with immediate effect.

At Chheda Specialities Foods, inspectors found workers mixing besan dough with bare hands and peeling bananas on contaminated floors beside decomposing waste.





The inspection also found fungal growth around edible oil tanks, wastewater on the processing floor, broken insect-proof mesh, dead houseflies, poor waste management and raw materials stored on wet, dusty floors. Multiple food samples collected during earlier inspections had already been declared unsafe or misbranded, with legal proceedings still underway.

The unit recorded a compliance score of 42%.

FSSAI said the licences have been suspended in the interest of public health and food safety. Chheda Specialities Foods will remain under suspension until it implements corrective measures and demonstrates full compliance with food safety regulations, while VKC Nuts' partial suspension will continue until further orders.

World.title: Explainer: What changes as Parliament passes Registration of Births and Deaths Bill
World.content:
The Parliament passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026, amid a wider logjam that has repeatedly disrupted the Monsoon Session. The Rajya Sabha cleared the legislation on Tuesday by voice vote days after the Lok Sabha passed it on July 31 amid opposition protests without a debate.

Both Houses witnessed repeated adjournments during the session, with several Bills being passed amid disruptions. The Monsoon Session began on July 20 and is scheduled to conclude on August 13.

The new legislation focuses on a seemingly routine but important part of government records like registering births and deaths. A birth certificate records a person's entry into the official system, while a death certificate formally records their departure.

Together, these documents help establish identity, maintain public records and provide proof for a range of legal and administrative purposes. The amendment seeks to tighten the process when such events are reported long after they occur.

What does the Bill change?

Under the existing system, delayed registration already requires additional verification. If information about a birth or death is submitted after one year but within two years, the amended law will require an order from a district magistrate, sub-divisional magistrate or an executive magistrate authorised by the district magistrate.





For cases reported more than two years after the event, the threshold becomes higher. The registration will require an order from a judicial magistrate of the First Class having jurisdiction over the place where the birth or death occurred.

The magistrate will have to verify the correctness of the information before permitting registration. A prescribed fee will also have to be paid, according to a document released by the government.

The amendment also updates the reference to an "Executive Magistrate" in the 1969 law to align it with the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the earlier Code of Criminal Procedure.

The government says the primary objective is to ensure that births and deaths are registered promptly and that delayed registrations are subjected to stronger scrutiny.

The Registration of Births and Deaths Act makes registration mandatory.

According to the government's statement of objects and reasons, birth and death certificates provide legal identity and can be used as evidence of a person's birth or death.

The government argues that the integrity of these records is particularly important because birth certificates can be used for several official purposes, including processes involving identity and citizenship-related documentation.

Tighter scrutiny of delayed registrations, it says, can help prevent fraudulent or questionable entries and improve the reliability of official records.

BJP IT cell head Amit Malviya said, âThe objective is straightforward: encourage timely registration, prevent fraudulent or dubious entries, and preserve the credibility of birth and death certificates, the foundational documents that establish a personâs legal identity.â

The government has also pointed to a significant rise in registration rates over the past decade.

Union minister of state for home Nityanand Rai said birth registration increased from 86.6% in 2014 to 99.1% in 2024, while death registration rose from 72.5% to 99.4% during the same period.

He also said around 3.5 lakh registration centres have been established across the country.

The government's argument is that as registration coverage approaches universal levels, the focus must increasingly be on ensuring that the remaining delayed or questionable cases are properly verified.

What is the significance of a birth certificate?

A birth certificate is often the first formal document linking an individual to the state. It records details such as a person's date and place of birth and can be required for a range of official purposes, including education, employment, passports and other government documentation.

The government has also highlighted the role of birth records in establishing identity and in processes where proof of birth or citizenship-related documentation is required.

That makes the accuracy of the registration system important beyond population statistics.

A fraudulent birth certificate, for instance, could potentially affect records across several government systems. Similarly, failure to register deaths can leave outdated information in official databases.

The government has also linked accurate death registration with keeping records, including electoral rolls, updated.

What happened in the Parliament?

The Lok Sabha passed the Bill on July 31 by voice vote amid opposition protests. Several opposition MPs entered the Well of the House demanding the presence of Union home minister

, and the legislation was cleared without a debate.

Parliamentary affairs minister

criticised the opposition for not participating in the proceedings and said the government wanted a discussion on the "important Bill".

âIt is unfortunate. Please do not repeat this in the future. People who sent you to Parliament will seek answers from you,â Rijiju said, urging MPs to participate in debates rather than disrupt proceedings.

The legislation was passed amid continued sloganeering, with the opposition MPs demanding the presence of Union home minister Amit Shah and his response on the "police action" against student protesters on July 20 at Jantar Mantar.

The Rajya Sabha later took up the Bill amid similar disruptions.

Moving the Bill in the Rajya Sabha, Rai said the government wanted every birth and death to be properly recorded. He said, âThe country wants that anyone born in the country, it is important that he or she is registered. Anyone who has died, cannot continue to remain in the voter lists to benefit some parties.â

Rai also linked the legislation to concerns over people who have died continuing to appear on electoral rolls.

The country now wants to get rid of ghosts. There are govts in some states that look for an opportunity and welcome those (who were not born in India) and register their births who are not eligible to be registered here. Now, we will not allow this to happen. Union minister of state for home Nityanand Rai

Encourage timely registration and prevent fraudulent or dubious entries.

He also cited the rise in registration rates as evidence of the government's efforts to improve the system.

Some NDA members supported the legislation. YSRCP member M R Reddy, AIADMK's M Thambidurai and BRS member Ravi Chandra Vaddiraju backed the Bill. BJP member Biswajit Sinha, meanwhile, accused the Congress of opposing the legislation because it did not want proper registration of births and deaths.

Sinha also referred to the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in West Bengal, claiming that people who had died years earlier remained on voter lists.

He alleged that some parties were helping illegal Bangladeshi and Pakistani infiltrators obtain birth registrations and voter identities, and said the proposed changes would help prevent such practices.

Leader of opposition

said, âThe prime minister and the home minister should come. we want discussion.â

Despite the protests, the Bill was taken up for consideration and passage.

Why did the opposition say

Opposition members did not reject the need for accurate birth and death records but questioned the practical implications of requiring a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class to approve registrations delayed by more than two years.

UPPL member Pramod Boro said the objective of the Bill was important but questioned whether an administrative responsibility should be shifted to the judiciary.

He warned that the provision could add to the workload of courts, increase costs and make registration more difficult for migrants, homeless people, poor families and those living in remote areas.

BJD member Santrupt Misra also questioned why registrations are delayed in the first place.

He suggested that the government should identify the reasons behind late registration and consider dedicated registration offices, particularly in tribal areas, to improve access.

CPI(M) member V Sivadasan supported the need for proper registration but said the government should also focus on the circumstances surrounding deaths, including malnutrition and student deaths.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The passage came amid a wider logjam in the Monsoon Session, with repeated adjournments in both Houses and several Bills being cleared amid disruptions.

With Parliament having passed the Bill, the legislation will now go through the remaining constitutional process before coming into force. The Bill, therefore, seeks to strike a balance between two objectives: ensuring that births and deaths are recorded promptly, while subjecting unusually delayed registrations to greater scrutiny.

World.title: JPSC, E20, anti-reservation: The issues India is talking about
World.content:
India just witnessed the 'reel' generation make the 'real' world listen. July 2026 saw something Indian parents have dreamt of for years: Gen Z looked up from its screens. But it was for a cause.

They turned memes into megaphones and forced the country to pay attention to exam reforms. In their own language, they ate and left no crumbs.

Exam paper leaks weren't new. Student protests weren't either. What was different was how a "cockroach" remark snowballed into a meme, then into the Cockroach Janata Party, and eventually into a nationwide movement that dominated headlines.

Now comes the bigger question: What other issues is India talking about?

Eyes on Jharkhand

While the

protest has ended, the demand for a system overhaul has not.

As Jantar Mantar went quiet, Jharkhand emerged as the new battleground as students demand accountability over JPSC-JSSC exam irregularities.

Student leader Devendra Nath Mahto has been on a hunger strike since August 2, while protesters are seeking an independent probe and reforms in the recruitment process.

E20

Then there is E20, a policy that directly affects vehicle owners.

The nationwide rollout of 20% ethanol-blended petrol has sparked a political and online debate over mileage, older vehicle compatibility and whether the Centre followed the phased roadmap laid out by NITI Aayog.





After the NEET protests, calls for Union minister Nitin Gadkari's resignation began circulating, while leaders including Arvind Kejriwal and

also raised the issue.

Vivek Rajput, a CA at a top government firm, says that although he has never attended a protest, this might become his first. âIf there is a protest over E20, I will definitely go. My vehicleâs mileage has gone down compared to before.â

CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka agrees that E20 deserves attention, but questions whether the government has adequately addressed concerns around its impact and benefits.

âObviously, E20 is an important issue that needs to be addressed. I don't think the government has very scientifically backed data to suggest whether the vehicles would be impacted or not,â Ranka said.

âNeither has there been any clarification on why the prices haven't dropped as it was promised to us. So what exactly has ethanol E20 petrol achieved in the country? There is no sort of clarity on that.â

Containers displayed as purported fuel samples are seen during an Indian Youth Congress (IYC) protest against E20 fuel policy (PTI)

Lack of jobs

Indiaâs job crisis is particularly acute among its growing pool of educated young people.

According to the State of Working India 2026 report, the number of young graduates rose nearly 13-fold from about 5 million in 1983 to 63 million in 2023, but graduate unemployment among those below 25 remains close to 40%. The number of unemployed graduates has also surged 16-fold, from less than 1 million to around 11 million over the same period.

Government data points to continued pressure: youth unemployment among 15-29-year-olds reached 16.2% in June 2026, even as their labour force participation rate fell to 40.3%.

The figures highlight a widening gap between the number of young people entering the workforce and the availability of secure, quality jobs.

Anger has also been growing over the increasing tax burden on common people. âAs the finance minister,

is not giving enough tax benefits to salaried people. Under the old tax regime, at least people could save money and also save on taxes. Now, neither are we able to save, nor are we getting tax benefits," said Rajput.

Anti-reservation movement

Reservation Hatao Andolan (RHA) recently gained nearly 6 million followers on Instagram. âBacked by citizens who feel left behind by reservation politics and driven by merit. The brave earn respect through their character and perseverance. Only the cowardly and the cruel keep shouting about caste,â the Insta bio of the page reads.

The page was formed in October last year and the first post was made in March this year.

Since the CJP protest, the account became more active.

RHAâs Insta page has gained significant followers

But quota has been a divisive issue in India. Unlike the paper-leak issue, which is an offence and affects students across categories, reservation is a constitutional policy rooted in questions of representation, historical disadvantage and unequal access â and does not attract a unified opinion.

The merit debate also gets complicated when cut-offs enter the picture.

In 2023, when the NEET-PG qualifying percentile was reduced to zero for all categories amid thousands of vacant seats, candidates who had fallen below the original cut-off became eligible for admission. General-category candidates accounted for the largest share of those admitted after the reduction â over 56%, compared with 26% OBC, 11% SC and 6% ST.

The skew was sharper in private colleges, where General-category candidates accounted for around 70% of those who secured clinical specialities after the cut-off was lowered.

The data does not suggest that General-category candidates were given a special concession; rather, it shows that they formed the largest share of those who benefited from the relaxation.

Caste-based reservation in education has been part of India's affirmative-action framework for decades. Before independence, several rulers and institutions had experimented with measures to uplift historically disadvantaged communities.

After independence, the Constitution formally provided for reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, which was later expanded to other backward classes and, in a different form, economically weaker sections.

Those advocating against the existing quota system argue that it compromises merit and should be replaced or reworked around economic disadvantage.

CJP's spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka brings focus on lack of jobs

RHA has posted five broad demands:

Income-based reservation: Under this, they demand that the reservation should purely be based on the income.

One family, one reservation, one time: Under this, it demands that once a family has benefited from reservation, the next generation should compete on merit.

Minimum standards for everyone: Under this, it demands that every exam should have minimum qualifying marks within 10-20% of the higher quota cut-off. If reserved seats fall vacant, it wants them allotted to the General category.

No reservation politics: Under this, it demands:

Political parties be barred from promising new or higher reservation quotas during elections.

The 50% limit on caste-based reservation should not be breached.

The sunset clause: Under this, it demands that no policy should run forever.

Set a time-bound roadmap to improve government schools, teachers and educational infrastructure.

As educational inequality reduces, reservation should be gradually phased out.

Reservation should be reviewed every 10 years using updated socio-economic data.

Reservation lists should be updated periodically, moving communities that have progressed to the General category.

CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka, however, believes the reservation debate itself risks taking attention away from a larger problem: the shortage of opportunities.

âI think the reservation-hatao movement, I just don't get the idea,â Ranka said. âThe focus every time the debate is brought on reservation, that really means that people, there is a distraction from the broader issue.â

For Ranka, that broader issue is jobs and seats. âThere are only 2% of the jobs which are government jobs in this country, 98% of the jobs in this country are private sector jobs,â he said. âWhy are there not enough jobs in this country? Why are there not enough government seats, medical seats, engineering seats in this country?â

âReservation, the topic of reservation is always a distraction on the broader structural issues which no one is ready to address.

We need more jobs, we need more seats in colleges. That's what people should be asking,â he said.

Others, however, see reservation itself as the issue that needs to be challenged.

The matter has gained even more attention after the UGC rules. The UGC equity regulations have also become a potential flashpoint, with the 2026 rules aimed at addressing discrimination in higher education.

Members of Swarn Samaj and Brahman Parivar stage a protest against the UGC's new caste-based equity rules at Hazratganj, in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh in January (PTI)

The Supreme Court stayed the regulations in January, citing ambiguities and the possibility of misuse, but the issue has resurfaced amid growing anti-reservation sentiment online and could emerge as another potential trigger for youth mobilisation.

But whether online traction can become a street movement remains an open question.

Rajput said his brother sent him the Reservation Hatao Andolan page on Instagram and he started following it only last week. He said there were 21 people on his team with eight or nine belonging to the General category while the others benefited from reservation.

For Rajput, however, the online movement has not yet translated into a willingness to protest on the ground.

That distinction could prove crucial. After all, CJP's success was not simply about getting people to watch, like or share.

But there is a counter-argument to the idea that reservation could become the next universal youth cause. Many SC/ST communities and other socially disadvantaged groups still lack equal access to quality education, particularly in rural areas where caste-based discrimination and social inequalities continue.

So, unlike the paper-leak issue, where the grievance could unite students across categories, an anti-reservation movement begins with a built-in fault line.

It may have the followers. It may have the slogans. It may even have people ready to take the fight to the streets. But whether it can replicate CJP's cross-sectional appeal is another question altogether.

Pollution

Diwali is just a couple of months away. And, as predictable as the festival itself, the annual debate will return: to burn or not to burn crackers.

But for Delhi-NCR, pollution is not just a seasonal social-media debate. When the air turns toxic, the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) kicks in, bringing curbs that can affect everything from construction and traffic to office timings and schools. A study by IITM-Pune and CAQM found that without GRAP, Delhi could see 60% more severe-AQI hours, while the measures could reduce PM2.5 levels by up to 42 Âµg/mÂ³, depending on the stage.

Anti-pollution protest: Protesters last year showing posters of Maoist commander Madvi Hidma, who was killed in an encounter (PTI)

In Mumbai too, pollution has emerged as a growing urban challenge, with construction and road dust, vehicle emissions and industrial activity among the key contributors to poor air quality. Pollution spikes have become a recurring concern, with several parts of the city recording AQI levels above 200, raising concerns over prolonged exposure to harmful particulate matter such as PM2.5. The problem adds to the wider challenges of rapid urbanisation, infrastructure growth and increasing vehicular traffic in the city.

So, could pollution become the next rallying point, or is an issue with no single villain simply too difficult to turn into a movement? âIf there is a protest over pollution, Iâll go for that too. I think we can raise our voice over issues that directly affect us. I would even join a protest over taxes,â said Rajput.

The logic is simple: if an issue hits your lungs, your wallet or your everyday life, it may be easier to turn outrage into action.

Poll Vote & Share your view Are you in favor of the E20 fuel policy? Yes, it's a good initiative No, it should be re-evaluated 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

So, what actually makes people protest?

For Ratna Singh, CJPâs legal head, the answer isn't simply the issue itself. It is how that issue is packaged, communicated and mobilised.

She believes CJP gained momentum because it was a Gen Z protest around education â an issue that extends well beyond NEET aspirants to competitive-exam candidates, school and college students, graduates and young people looking for jobs.

Education, she said, allowed both Gen Z and Gen Alpha â and even their parents â to relate to the movement.

âA lot of people in the crowd, when they were coming, they were like, you know, my parents were not letting me be here. But now I'm here. So they're also supporting,â Singh said.

And then comes the part that may matter most for the next protest. âSomething can trend on Instagram, but on ground, how you are planning it, how you are strategising it, that's also important,â Singh said.

She added that people may relate to an issue online but still not turn up physically.

How organisers convey the importance of an issue â and how they plan to keep an agitation going â can determine whether it survives beyond a social-media trend.

Why CJP clicked with Indiaâs youth: Anger, accessibility and a platform to be heard

That is perhaps the biggest lesson from CJP.

Going viral can get an issue noticed. Mobilising people can turn it into a movement.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Singh believes unemployment could be the next major youth issue. CJP is planning a nationwide âKya Bolti Publicâ campaign in September to hear from young people across states about the problems they face.

She said the organisation wants unemployment and education to become a more central part of the public conversation and wants to understand youth concerns and push for reforms. âWith the success of Cockroach Janata Party, this wave has started, where people will come forward, people will talk about issues, people will also talk about unemployment and youth-related, youth-centric issues,â Singh said.

Reservation has the Instagram audience. Pollution has the lived experience. E20 has the everyday grievance. Unemployment has the scale. But whichever issue wins the race will need to clear one final hurdle. It has to make people look up from their screens â and then actually leave them.

World.title: 21 of 57 TN MPs attend CM Vijay’s meet, reject Delimitation Bill; DMK, AIADMK stay away
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu MPs on Saturday "unanimously" decided to oppose Centre's Delimitation Bill after chief minister C Joseph Vijay chaired a meeting to discuss its likely impact on the state.Congress MP Karti Chidambaram said around 21 out of 57 Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha MPs attended the meeting and agreed to resist any alteration in Tamil Nadu's representation in Parliament."The chief minister of Tamil Nadu had called for a meeting for all the MPs from Tamil Nadu from both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. About 21 of us attended the meeting, and there was absolute unanimity that Tamil Nadu's rights must be preserved. Our representation in Parliament can't be diminished. Any kind of alteration and delimitation, either on the basis of population or on a proportionate increase, will be resisted," Chidambaram said."We want Parliament to be frozen at 543, and the distribution among the states to be preserved as it is, which means Tamil Nadu will have 39 members in a House of 543. We are clear in our unanimous opinion that a larger Parliament will be an ineffective Parliament, and Tamil Nadu will not be well served by a larger Parliament.So we want Parliament to be preserved at 543 with the same representation of 39 Lok Sabha MPs for Tamil Nadu," he added.The meeting was boycotted by the DMK and AIADMK, which dismissed the deliberations as a "farce" and a "drama".The meeting was held at Kalaivanar Arangam, a government-owned auditorium near the Secretariat.Senior DMK leader A Raja told reporters in Perambalur that it was "a farce, a laughable exercise", arguing that the TVK government was deliberating on an issue about which it had no clarity.Meanwhile, AIADMK called the meeting a "hurriedly staged drama", pointing out that no new delimitation Bill had been introduced in Parliament and there had been no official announcement on the exercise.While the Congress and other opposition parties have supported the Women's Reservation Bill, they have opposed linking its implementation to the delimitation exercise. The opposition has demanded that women's reservation be delinked from delimitation.The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023, was passed by both Houses of Parliament. However, its implementation has not moved forward after the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill fell in the Lok Sabha on April 17, failing to secure the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of members present and voting.The Bill linked the implementation of 33 percent women's reservation in legislatures to delimitation of Lok Sabha constituencies.

World.title: Delhi to set up modern housing facility for children in conflict with law
World.content:
The Department of Women and Child Development (WCD) has submitted a proposal to the Public Works Department (PWD) for an integrated 8-acre residential facility in Alipur to house at least 700 children in conflict with law (CCL) and asked the PWD to prepare a cost estimate.

A CCL is a person below the age of 18 who is alleged or found to have committed an offence.

The proposed facility in the north-west Delhi suburb has been envisioned as a modern residential unit with classrooms, skill development and vocational training centres, sports and recreational facilities, healthcare services, digital learning facilities and dedicated counselling spaces.

As per the WCD proposal, the integrated facility, which would house at least 700 children aged seven and above, would have 52 dormitories and 10 classrooms with digital facilities. “As per our estimate, around 175 people, including 28 educators and 14 psychologists and counsellors, would be needed to run it,” a WCD official said.

The official added, “The inmates will be enrolled in various skill development and diploma courses offered by the Delhi Institute of Hotel Management and Catering Technology.”

Chief Minister Rekha Gupta had announced such a facility during a speech in February. “It will not be a punitive institution but will rather be developed with the objective of providing a safe environment, a dignified life and opportunities for reform,” Ms. Gupta had said.

Comprehensive care

WCD Secretary Rashmi Singh said, “The proposed facility will have a dedicated mental health unit with qualified counsellors, psychologists and other mental health professionals to provide comprehensive psychosocial care and rehabilitation support.”

She added that the residents will be grouped by age (7-12, 13-15 and 16-18) and gender (male and female) to avoid conflicts and vulnerabilities.

To support the rehabilitation of the occupants, the WCD has partnered with the Khadi and Village Industries Commission to provide vocational training in air conditioner and refrigerator repair, pottery, papad and spice making, and signed an MoU with an NGO to promote adolescent development through structured sports and life skills programmes, as well as outreach activities.

Currently, Delhi has five ‘observation homes’, two ‘places of safety’ and one ‘special home’ for CCL. These are located at Sewa Kutir Complex, Delhi Gate Complex, Majnu Ka Tila and Nirmal Chhaya Complex.

An observation home is a temporary residential facility where CCL are held while their case is heard before a Juvenile Justice Board (JJB). A special home is where juveniles who are found to have committed an offence are sent for rehabilitation and reform. A place of safety is where those aged 16 to 18 who are found to have committed heinous crimes are kept.

Significant challenges

People working with the children at these homes said such facilities face significant challenges. “Overcrowding is a challenge. There is a shortage of social workers, psychologists and educators. Psychological first aid and counselling services need to improve significantly,” said Ravi Kant, the national convener of Just Rights for Children that runs an Observation Home in Delhi.

Under the Juvenile Justice Rules, 2016, the prescribed staff strength is about 15 personnel, including a superintendent, a medical officer and a nurse, trained counsellors or psychologists, and other staff, including rehabilitation-cum-placement officers, educators, probation officers, child welfare officers, case workers and PT-cum-Yoga instructors.

“Due to staff shortage, the quality of care and counselling provided is basic. Moreover, the employees at such facilities are not sensitised or trained to deal with children who need special care, such as those facing trauma,” said Rita Singh, a former member of the Delhi Commission for Protection of Child Rights.

As per official data, Delhi has a Special Juvenile Police Unit in almost every district, with over 400 Child Welfare Police Officers serving at 225 police stations. The city also has nearly 800 Probation Officers.

Delhi has seven JJBs across seven districts. “The JJBs are overloaded with cases. With just seven JJBs in 11 districts, you can imagine how much time each child must be given,” Ms. Rita Singh said.

World.title: Several WhatsApp users say their accounts 'put under review'
World.content:
Instant messaging app WhatsApp on Monday (August 3, 2026) put multiple accounts, including those in India, "under review" for 24 hours and blocked all the app features, prompting several affected users to flag the issue through social media.

When contacted, a WhatsApp spokesperson said, "We are always working to stay ahead of those trying to abuse our service and ban accounts to help keep other users safe. Sometimes we get this wrong and if we do, we try to fix it as quickly as possible to get people back to chatting."

The disruption was highlighted around 8 p.m. IST when users started facing the issue without any prior warning from the Meta group's messaging app.

The WhatsApp app on the screen displayed the message, "Account in review. Date requested: 3 Aug 2026. Your account activity and device info is being checked to make sure it follows our terms of service. We will notify you of the result typically within 24 hours."

Below these remarks, the app shows an option to learn about account issues, which include, "How to use WhatsApp responsibly. See guidance" and an option, "About stolen phone and accounts".

Some of the users on social media posted different messages.

"My WhatsApp account has been disabled without any explanation. I have already submitted an appeal, but the review page only displays a generic message stating that it will "typically be reviewed within 24 hours. Help me urgently," a user said on social media.

An account on X by the name of Saloni posted, "My WhatsApp account was suddenly disabled without any warning. I only use the official app, and my work depends on WhatsApp. Please help. This was so unnecessary."

World.title: Fire breaks out at electronic chip unit in Noida, two firefighters killed, three injured
World.content:
A massive fire broke out at an electronic chip manufacturing unit in Noida, killing two firefighters and injuring three others, police said on Tuesday (August 4, 2026).

The incident occurred late on Monday (August 3) night at the ILGIM company in the Ecotech-3 industrial area, where at least six fire brigade vehicles were rushed after information about the blaze was received, a police spokesperson said.

The firefighters were attempting to douse the blaze when a wall and an iron beam inside the factory suddenly collapsed, injuring five of them, the spokesperson said.

All five injured firefighters were immediately taken to a hospital by ambulance, where Rohit Yadav and Tirathpal Singh succumbed to their injuries, he said.

The condition of the three other injured firefighters - Rajpal Singh, Manish Kumar and Amit Kumar - is stated to be out of danger and they are undergoing treatment, the spokesperson said.

Senior police officers, along with a team of the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), are present at the spot, he said.

The cause of the fire is being investigated and necessary legal action is being taken, police said.

World.title: BJP rule hurting Hindus, says SDPI national president M.K. Faizy
World.content:
Social Democratic Party of India (SDPI) national president M.K. Faizy said that the BJP-led Union government was a heavily failed administration.

Speaking to reporters here after chairing a State-level party meeting here on Saturday, he added that the Union government had previously faced setbacks within Parliament and is now confronting public disapproval over issues such as the leakage of NEET examination question papers.

He stated that this has impacted citizens across all communities, including Hindus.

“Although the BJP came to power promising to safeguard the Hindu population, the grim reality today is that Hindus are being harmed by the party’s actions,” he stated.

He added that the theft at the Ayodhya Ram Temple served as a major illustration of this failure.

Above all, the youth have waged a major protest against the Union government. As a fallout, Dharmendra Pradhan, who was a Union Minister, has stepped down.

“He had been in the office for 12 years. He has fallen as the first wicket. If this continues as it is, a situation will come in 2029 where all wickets of the BJP will fall and they will lose,” Mr. Faizy noted.

Currently, the SDPI party plays a major role in the protests being conducted nationwide against the Union government, he observed.

“In Tamil Nadu, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam leader and Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay has started a party and even formed the government,” he said.

But, in Kerala, though everyone enjoys watching Mr. Vijay’s films and he has a lot of fans there, that alone will not work out in politics, he remarked.

“The people of Kerala are capable of separating cinema and politics. They will think and decide whom to vote for,” he added.

SDPI State president Nellai Mubarak among others were present during the event.

World.title: Maharashtra issues order on safe food in schools
World.content:
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration has issued a compliance order for all schools in the State to ensure the provision of safe and balanced food. The order applies to all government, aided, and private schools, including those affiliated with state, CBSE, and ICSE boards, and covers pre-primary to secondary levels, residential schools, hostels, canteens, and food suppliers.
