Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.title: Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.content:
China’s industry associations are revoking hundreds of honorary designations that have increasingly been used as marketing tools.

In late July, the China Cuisine Association announced that all previously awarded titles — including “Chinese Culinary Master” and “Chinese Catering Service Master” — along with related certificates and uniforms, were now invalid. The association also revoked all honorary designations awarded to cities — such as the “capital of” and “hometown of” certain dishes. Local governments are now officially barred from using them in any form of publicity.

The revocation of the titles triggered renewed interest among social media users. This week, they questioned the reliability of the “National Stir-Fried Meat King” title awarded to restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, after discovering it was conferred following an online public vote on photos and videos submitted by contestants.

The title has not yet been revoked, though, in response, the China Cuisine Association said they will “communicate after reviewing relevant materials,” domestic media reported.

Originally intended to recognize exceptional craftsmanship, “master” titles were once rare state honors. But in the early 2000s, industry associations across the tea, ceramics, and jewelry sectors, and many others, began creating their own titles, allowing businesses to charge a premium by creating the perception of higher-quality products and services. However, numerous shadowy practices also emerged around the honors, including honorary title certificates being openly sold on e-commerce platforms.

Since the beginning of this year, at least a dozen national and local industry associations covering sectors ranging from cosmetic surgery to jade carving and wedding services have revoked or abolished previously-conferred honorary titles containing words like “master.”

An increasing number of industry associations began nullifying their own honorary titles after the Social Work Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Ministry of Civil Affairs jointly released new guidelines on governing social organizations’ awards and commendations in mid-July.

The guidelines, which took effect on Aug. 1, imposed stricter eligibility requirements on organizations seeking to present awards. It also prohibits organizations from charging fees for recognition programs or partnering with, or outsourcing such activities to, for-profit entities.

China has gradually tightened oversight of awards and commendations organized by social organizations over the past decade, with its first regulations governing the practice taking effect in 2012.

Restrictions were tightened further in 2018, when award programs using national designations such as “China,” “Chinese,” and “national” became subject to stricter controls. In 2022, authorities required organizations seeking to launch honorary recognition programs to hold at least a 4A rating, the second highest on the country’s social organization rating scale.

Lu Zhen, a lawyer at the Shanghai office of Beijing-based Hylands Law Firm, told local media that rather than eliminating professional evaluations altogether, the regulations are intended to draw a clearer distinction between professional qualifications and commercialized honorary awards.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: An  for restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, at a shopping mall in Beijing, May 23, 2024. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018862/Skin in the Game: What Makes a Chinese Game Character Feel Real?
World.title: Skin in the Game: What Makes a Chinese Game Character Feel Real?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018862/Skin in the Game: What Makes a Chinese Game Character Feel Real?
World.content:
Ask anyone to name a Chinese video game character, and chances are they will say Chun-Li. That is both her achievement and the problem.

When Japanese gaming giant Capcom debuted her character in the 1991 arcade game Street Fighter II, Chun-Li was an Interpol officer. But it was her blue qipao, double buns, and devastating kicks that made her famous.

Those details made Chun-Li instantly recognizable, but they also turned her Chinese identity into spectacle — graceful, formidable, and framed for the male gaze. Her image was already so familiar by 1993 that Jackie Chan could parody her in his film “City Hunter” without explanation.

The arcade era rewarded that kind of instant legibility. Fighting-game characters were built from bold silhouettes, familiar archetypes, and minimal backstory. In Japanese developer SNK’s 1994 arcade fighting game The King of Fighters ’94, Chin Gentsai was the drunken, disheveled old man cast as the quintessential kung fu master. Chinese culture was visible, but largely reduced to type: exotic, recognizable, and stripped of psychological depth.

It would take another generation of games for Chinese characters to move beyond such tropes. By the mid-2010s, globally popular multiplayer titles were reaching vast Chinese audiences, whose size and commercial importance made their expectations harder to ignore. As Chinese characters became more common, players increasingly expected them to feel culturally grounded rather than assembled from stock signs.

When American video game developer Blizzard released the first-person shooter Overwatch in 2016, its Chinese hero, Mei-Ling Zhou, seemed to mark a step beyond the old archetypes. A climatologist from Xi’an in northwestern China, Mei wears polar expedition gear and is portrayed as affable, resilient, and determined to protect both people and the planet.

Yet while Mei is more fully drawn than the arcade characters before her, her Chinese identity remains largely incidental. Her nationality adds diversity to Overwatch’s global cast without meaningfully shaping her inner life.

Nearly a decade later, Overwatch introduced its second Chinese hero, Wuyang Ye. A 19-year-old from the southwestern Sichuan province, he attends the fictional Wuxing University, whose colleges draw on the five traditional Chinese elements. Yet the most revealing detail is also the most ordinary: Wuyang is a college student, a figure immediately familiar to much of the game’s Chinese audience.

Overwatch also gave its characters linguistic markers of where they came from. In the English-language version, an allied Mei shouts “Freeze, don’t move!” when using her ultimate ability; an enemy Mei delivers the warning in Mandarin. For Chinese players, the switch allowed her nationality to be heard rather than merely listed in her biography.

By the time Wuyang appeared, simply hearing a Chinese character speak Chinese was no longer enough. In a 2025 promotional trailer, he dismisses a challenge with “xiao case,” a Chinese-English expression roughly equivalent to “piece of cake.” Some Chinese viewers found the line playful; others argued that a student from Sichuan should instead use the local expression “le ge hao long” — “this one’s easy.”

The disagreement was minor, but it showed how expectations had changed. Players expected his language to reflect where he came from and who he was.

In 2026, Wuyang’s elder sister, Anran Ye, joined the Overwatch roster. Associated with the element of fire, she is forceful, impatient, and quick to challenge her younger brother. Their exchanges introduce sibling rivalry, parental pressure, and family expectations, giving both characters a social world beyond their individual backstories.

This marks the clearest break from Mei. Mei’s Chinese identity is conveyed largely through nationality and language; the Ye siblings’ emerges through family relationships and everyday behavior. Anran feels familiar not as a symbol of China but as the demanding older sister who refuses to let her younger brother coast.

The 2020 tactical shooter Valorant, developed by U.S. video game company Riot Games — owned by Chinese tech giant Tencent — offers a different kind of Chinese character. Sage is built around protection rather than aggression: she heals injured teammates, raises defensive barriers, and can revive fallen allies. Players often call her “mom,” a playful nickname rooted less in her nationality than in the trust inspired by her abilities and calm authority.

Three years later, Valorant introduced its second Chinese character, Iso, a hired gun from the southwestern megacity of Chongqing. His abilities are built around single combat, allowing him to isolate opponents and force them into one-on-one fights. The contrast with Sage is immediate: Sage protects and restores her team, while Iso is aggressive, self-contained, and designed to fight alone.

Iso’s reveal trailer featured “Renegade,” an original track by Chinese rappers 99 God and C103, grounding the character in contemporary Chinese music without relying on traditional costume or martial-arts imagery.

Neither character is expected to represent China as a whole or reduced to a single cultural type. Together with Mei, Wuyang, and Anran, they mark a broader shift in global competitive games, where Chinese characters increasingly appear as individuals rather than national symbols.

Chinese culture has also become more visible beyond character rosters. In League of Legends, developed by Riot Games, and Honor of Kings, developed in China by Tencent’s TiMi Studio Group, players can buy skins inspired by Chinese mythology, clothing, and decorative motifs.

But visibility alone was not enough. Anran’s trailer presented her as fierce and commanding, while her in-game model appeared cuter and more delicate.

Chinese players objected to the mismatch, and Blizzard later announced changes to the design. The response showed that players were judging not merely whether Chinese elements were present but whether the character remained consistent with the world and personality the game had established.

From Chun-Li to the Ye siblings, and from Sage to Iso, Chinese characters in global competitive games have begun to move from spectacle to self. They are no longer recognized only through costume, accent, or archetype. Players now debate how they speak, how they look, where they come from, and whether those details add up to a convincing person.

In the years ahead, perhaps the misty canal towns of Jiangnan, in eastern China’s lower Yangtze region, will appear on a new arena map, Miao embroidery on a tournament skin, or Tang dynasty poetry woven into a champion’s identity. But such details will matter only when they do more than decorate.

When culture is lived rather than labeled, a Chinese figure stops being a symbol. They become someone players can root for, and perhaps someone who brings them closer to their own roots.

(Header image: Visuals from Street Fighter, Blizzard, and Riot Game, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018857/Do the Math: Why China’s First Fields Medals Are Just the Beginning
World.title: Do the Math: Why China’s First Fields Medals Are Just the Beginning
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018857/Do the Math: Why China’s First Fields Medals Are Just the Beginning
World.content:
When Wang Hong and Deng Yu became the first Chinese nationals to receive the Fields Medal — the so-called “Nobel Prize for mathematics” — on July 23, few people were as pleased as Shing-Tung Yau.

“For China’s math community, this is something we’ve hoped to see for decades,” Yau, a Chinese American mathematician who was awarded the Fields Medal in 1982, tells The Paper.

“It gives us new hope. We can now envision the day when decisive breakthroughs are made by scholars trained entirely in China and are carried out on Chinese soil.”

Yau is the founding dean of Tsinghua University’s Qiuzhen College, which was established in early 2021 to strengthen the cultivation of mathematical talent. One of its flagship initiatives, the YAU Mathematical Sciences Leaders Program, recruits gifted high school-age students from around the world, placing them on an eight-year track running from bachelor’s degree to Ph.D.

In recent years, however, a training industry has emerged around admission to the college, with some parents viewing it as a shortcut to one of China’s top universities. Public scrutiny also intensified in July when several recruits reportedly faced expulsion during the initial preparatory semester after failing to meet Qiuzhen’s academic standards.

In interviews, Yau has openly criticized China’s long-standing reliance on math competitions and commercial test-prep programs, saying that they only make students proficient in taking exams and standardized problem-solving routines, which has had “an extremely negative impact on the development of mathematical talent.”

He reveals that the college is planning a comprehensive overhaul of its admissions and exam systems, with the aim of enrolling students who truly love mathematics, not those solely motivated by the desire to enter an elite university.

Following Wang and Deng’s accomplishment, Yau now hopes China can cultivate many homegrown scholars within the next decade who can forge their own intellectual paths and produce work that shapes the direction of mathematics worldwide.

Here, Yau talks with The Paper about his feelings on math education, basic research, and scientific innovation.

The Paper: How should we understand the importance of basic research?

Yau: People have various understandings of basic research. In my view, basic research should make meaningful contributions to the nation and society. China faces many technological bottlenecks, and we scientists have a responsibility to help overcome them.

At the same time, we cannot remain content with following in the footsteps of others. If we’re always solving problems that others have defined, merely improving on existing work, then even if we eventually surpass them, we are still allowing someone else to set the agenda. There is certainly a place for this kind of research, but it cannot be the whole story.

People often say that China is good at taking innovation from “2 to 100” — refining and scaling existing ideas — but lacks the capacity for “0-to-1” breakthroughs: original discoveries that set new directions.

Some lines of inquiry may appear to have little practical value today. Yet pursuing them can deepen our understanding of the laws of nature, and that deeper understanding can lay the groundwork for transformative discoveries. Above all, curiosity is the driving force behind 0-to-1 innovation.

When scientists began investigating quantum phenomena in the early 20th century, their goal was to unravel the mysteries of atomic structure and quantum effects. No one imagined that this research would revolutionize electronics, industrial technologies, and countless other fields, reshaping the modern world. Even today, many of the technological challenges that constrain China’s development are rooted in areas closely connected to quantum mechanics.

That is why basic research must serve two purposes simultaneously: address the pressing challenges facing the country while safeguarding the freedom to pursue curiosity-driven research.

The Paper: Why does China seem to lag behind in 0-to-1 innovation, and what is the solution?

Yau: In many areas, once someone else opens up an important new direction, Chinese scientists move in quickly and, in many cases, improve on it or even outperform the first pioneers. But genuinely new fields that we ourselves have initiated from the outset remain exceedingly rare. Taking that first original step is the most important challenge facing the development of basic research.

The history of mathematics offers many examples of theories that were initially misunderstood or dismissed, only to have their significance recognized years later. Yet many young researchers lack the courage to pursue this kind of work.

One reason is that such research requires extraordinary patience. An unconventional idea may take five or six years before its value becomes apparent. During that time, researchers might struggle to secure even basic funding, and their career advancement could suffer. Most people naturally shy away from such risks.

Also, basic research is inherently a long-term endeavor. It rarely produces immediate rewards, so many people lose interest over time. But genuine interest cannot be manufactured overnight — it must be cultivated from an early age. We need to inspire young people to develop a love of scholarship and a sense of wonder about nature. Without that inner drive, it is impossible to nurture first-rate researchers.

Many people’s aspiration for pursuing research has changed. Increasingly, scholarship is viewed as a means to acquire academic titles or prestigious appointments. When my generation entered academia, there was no option but to keep moving forward. By contrast, young people today generally enjoy far greater material security, yet they face intense external pressures that make them more vulnerable to anxiety. At the same time, parents and society have become overly protective of children. Only by changing the broader culture of scientific research can China achieve genuine success in basic research and produce truly original breakthroughs.

The Paper: Does this also point to shortcomings in China’s system for evaluating academic research?

Yau: In some respects, our system for encouraging academic research places too much emphasis on material incentives and too little on the intrinsic value of scholarship. At some universities, generous salaries and housing allowances are reserved primarily for scholars with fancy titles. As a result, many young researchers feel compelled to chase these credentials rather than focus on the pursuit of knowledge.

Another issue is that China’s academic evaluation system makes relatively little use of international peer review. At Harvard University, for example, tenure decisions are based on assessments from leading scholars around the world. In China, evaluations are often confined to domestic experts, and in some cases only to reviewers at the same institution.

China has relatively few researchers capable of achieving genuine 0-to-1 innovation — but the situation is changing. Many scholars returning from overseas have brought back new ideas, research cultures, and methodological approaches. That does not mean China must rely indefinitely on talent trained abroad. Outstanding scholars are also emerging from within the country. The key is to ensure that decisions are guided by experts who truly understand the field. Ultimately, we must chart our own course, but we should at least listen carefully to those with expertise.

Even where international evaluation has been introduced, many Chinese universities continue to judge research primarily by metrics such as publication counts and journal impact factors. Those measures are poorly suited to evaluating the most original and exploratory forms of research.

We need to encourage young scholars in Chinese universities to set their sights much higher. At the very least, a small but significant group should aspire to become world-leading researchers — people capable of producing groundbreaking work that shapes the direction of mathematics, and even basic research more broadly, for decades to come.

The Paper: China’s total research and development spending exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan ($581 billion) in 2025. Investment in basic research accounted for 7% of that, a record high but still far below the 15-20% seen in many developed countries. How do you view this gap?

Yau: Research cannot be driven solely by immediate applications or by what may prove useful over the next five years. Basic research must not be neglected simply because its practical impact is delayed. More often than not, its true significance becomes apparent only after 10, 20 years, or even longer.

In fact, basic research is not especially expensive. Most fundamental research relies on thinking, reasoning, and mathematical deduction; its principal resources are the minds of scholars. Although some experimental fields like high-energy physics require substantial investment, China’s major research institutions are fully capable of supporting such work.

Generally speaking, allocating around 10% of total national R&D spending to the most fundamental areas of basic science would be sufficient. What matters most is that we take a long-term view and invest not only for today’s needs but also for the future.

The Paper: You have long advocated identifying and nurturing talented young students. Why is this important for basic research?

Yau: I have been at Qiuzhen College for five years. Every Monday, I teach a course on the history of math, focusing on the most influential mathematicians of the past three centuries and the paths they took in their intellectual development. Almost all of them developed a passion for math at the age of 12 or 13.

The future of China’s basic sciences depends on such young people, too. At that age, their minds are not yet constrained by established thinking; they possess tremendous intellectual flexibility. But as people grow older, their habits of thought become more fixed, making it more difficult to produce the kind of 0-to-1 innovation that opens new frontiers. That is why identifying and cultivating exceptional talent must begin early.

Some people argue that this approach runs counter to the principles of compulsory education or educational fairness. But requiring every student to meet exactly the same standard can, in fact, bury the rare young talents we most need to nurture. That would be the greatest injustice of all.

We should establish a systematic mechanism for identifying and developing the small fraction of students with exceptional gifts, providing them with specialized education. That is consistent with the educational principle of teaching students according to their individual abilities, and that is what genuine fairness looks like.

The Paper: What qualities do you feel define a true scientist?

Yau: A scientist must possess an open mind and a broad intellectual outlook, and they must build a rigorous academic foundation. No matter how difficult it may be, the fundamentals must be mastered — and math is especially important. Interdisciplinary learning and cultivating the humanities are also important. We should strive for broadly educated scholars rather than narrow specialists.

Original thinking is key. American students often ask unusual, even eccentric, questions. That curiosity is fascinating, and it frequently leads them to creative research. Chinese students, by contrast, tend to be more inclined to follow established rules and are often reluctant to question accepted ideas. We should protect their curiosity, encourage them to think boldly, and give them the confidence to ask questions.

Ultimately, the spirit of science is about seeking to understand the mysteries of nature and uncovering the objective laws that govern the universe — not about pursuing fame or prestige.

We should create an environment in which researchers are free to explore nature and pursue scholarship out of genuine intellectual curiosity, allowing them to remain true to that original motivation. Young scientists should not spend their careers chasing academic titles or even a Nobel Prize. The purpose of scholarship is to discover the truth and beauty of the natural world.

Reported by Teng Han.

A version of this Q&A originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: A collage shows Shing-Tung Yau in 2025 (left), and Wang Hong (center) and Deng Yu in 2026. Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018861/Video Game Accounts Can Be Inherited, Chinese Court Rules
World.title: Video Game Accounts Can Be Inherited, Chinese Court Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018861/Video Game Accounts Can Be Inherited, Chinese Court Rules
World.content:
A Beijing court has ruled in favor of a mother seeking to inherit her late son’s 87 online gaming accounts, selecting the dispute as an example case to provide judges with legal direction on similar future proceedings involving digital assets.

The case, reported Monday by the People’s Court Daily, a newspaper affiliated with China’s Supreme People’s Court, involved the inheritance rights to the accounts of an avid gamer surnamed Gu, who passed away last year at 36 due to oral cancer.

With China’s internet penetration rate reaching 80.1% by the end of 2025, the case comes as the country faces increasing pressure to handle the growing volume of digital assets left behind by deceased users.

Since China’s Civil Code — which states that digital assets are protected by law — took effect in 2021, courts have increasingly recognized the property value of digital assets. In 2025, the Supreme People’s Court created a separate case category for disputes involving data and online virtual property.

Between 2010 and 2021, Gu registered accounts on games by Chinese game developer Changyou, acquiring valuable in-game assets due to having “built up the accounts” over the years, according to the report.

After Gu’s passing, his mother, surnamed Chen, asked the company to transfer the accounts into her name so she could sell them to help cover her living expenses, as she relied on a low income and no family support.

The company denied her request, however, citing their user agreement, which states that it retains ownership of all account-related data, including account information, game characters, virtual items, and in-game currency.

Chen then sued the company. In April, the Beijing Shijingshan District People’s Court ruled that although ownership of the accounts rested with the company, the accounts had independent economic value because Gu had invested time, effort, and money in them. As a result, the court found that the right of use of the accounts, though not their ownership, could be inherited.

The court ordered the company to complete the transfer of the accounts’ real-name registration to Chen within 15 days after the ruling took effect. Chen is the sole legal heir to the accounts, as Gu’s daughter waived her inheritance rights.

Many online platforms prohibit account transfers or inheritance. But platforms’ user agreements cannot override a user’s legal inheritance rights, Zhang Yingzhou, the judge presiding over the case, told local media.

“Heirs inherit the economic interests attached to the right to use an account, not ownership of the account itself,” the judge said.

Other incidents related to the transfer of digital assets have made headlines in China recently, including a case related to the recycling of popular Chinese-American singer Coco Lee’s phone number by her telecom operator after she committed suicide in 2023.

In 2025, a user who registered for domestic music streaming platform NetEase with a newly purchased mobile phone number was inadvertently logged into Lee’s verified artist account. NetEase explained that the phone number originally linked to Lee’s account had been reassigned to a new user without unbinding the account link to NetEase. The incident sparked widespread discussion on domestic social media about digital privacy, account security, and the management of digital assets after death.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018856/The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.title: The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018856/The Chinese Factory Town Betting on America’s Mahjong Boom
World.content:
JIANGSU, East China — “We are looking for a factory that can produce acrylic mahjong tiles.”

Hua Fangyi repeated that pitch at nearly 30 factories in Taixing, a city in eastern China’s Jiangsu province known for manufacturing mahjong tiles. “Almost every factory refused,” she says.

After quitting her job to start an export business last October, Hua, 28, spotted a surge in overseas demand for American mahjong. Believing the opportunity might last only a few months, she planned to test the market with just a few dozen sets.

But Taixing’s factories were built for large runs of traditional Chinese mahjong, not the small batches of brightly colored acrylic tiles overseas buyers wanted. Some produced only conventional melamine sets; others required minimum orders far beyond what Hua could afford.

Then Hua found a factory with 20 American mahjong sets in stock. She bought the entire batch, and it sold out almost immediately.

Within months, she had built a company shipping more than 5,000 sets a month and generating roughly $400,000 in monthly sales. Across Taixing, factories that had once turned away from American mahjong were now chasing the same overseas buyers.

“Almost every factory is now making American mahjong,” Hua says.

The shift came as rising material costs and intensifying competition squeezed margins on traditional sets. Overseas demand offered higher returns, prompting established factories to buy equipment, hire workers, and adapt their production lines to the elaborate designs sought by American buyers.

The opportunity has also drawn a new generation of entrepreneurs to Taixing: former tech workers, salespeople, and export traders hoping to manufacture the tiles and build brands of their own.

Together, they are all betting on a boom whose limits remain unclear. For now, overseas orders have given Taixing’s mahjong industry fresh momentum, sending an old manufacturing center racing to master a game it barely recognized a year ago.

Follow the dots

Growing up around her family’s garment factory and later working in international e-commerce at Alibaba, Hua had experience with both manufacturing and overseas sales. She began searching for products that could find a market abroad.

She continued using the habits she developed in product operations, tracking trends on social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook and monitoring sales performance on overseas independent websites. American mahjong stood out.

The game itself, however, has a long history in the U.S. The governing body for American mahjong, the National Mah Jongg League, was founded in 1937 with 32 members; it now has more than 350,000 members and publishes a new card of official hands and rules each year.

More recently, American brands such as Oh My Mahjong have helped recast mahjong tiles as colorful, premium lifestyle products, while influencers and social clubs have brought the game to younger players seeking in-person connection.

In April 2026, review platform Yelp reported that U.S. searches for mahjong clubs had jumped 4,467% between September 2024 and August 2025, compared with the previous 12 months. Oh My Mahjong’s sets now sell for $350 to $475, with most priced around $400 — versus the roughly 100 yuan ($15) many Chinese sets sell for in China on e-commerce platform Taobao.

But Hua initially expected the opportunity to be short-lived. Without historical data on American mahjong, she looked to previous domestic product cycles, which often peaked around specific festivals. She expected demand to surge around Christmas, just two months after she first spotted the trend.

Moving quickly to find a supplier, Hua and her father, who runs the family’s garment factory, drove several hundred kilometers from Ningbo, in neighboring Zhejiang province, to Taixing.

But many workshops had no obvious signs and appeared on maps only under broad categories such as “entertainment products.” From the road, little revealed what was being made inside.

Hua struggled to understand the local dialect, so her father asked residents and security guards where they could find factory owners. “We’d only know we’d found the right place after spotting a set or two of mahjong tiles,” she says. “They’d point us to a building and a floor, and we’d keep looking until we found the boss.”

The industry was all around them. A search for “mahjong” on Qichacha, a Chinese corporate database, returns nearly 180 businesses in Taixing, many of them small workshops specializing in a single stage of production.

The cluster grew from a household trade dating to the 1980s, when local families cut and polished tiles by hand from bamboo and ox bone. Over time, production split among specialized workshops handling tile blanks, engraving, polishing, printing, and packaging.

“If one family made money from it, the neighbors would learn too,” says Zhu Ronggen, whose father was among Taixing’s earliest mahjong makers. “One person taught another, and slowly the whole village started making mahjong.”

Zhu grew up inside that manufacturing network. After studying mechanical engineering, he returned to Taixing in 2015 and opened his own factory. By the following year, he was producing traditional sets for China’s domestic market.

So when a customer first asked him to make an American set, Zhu, now 48, assumed it would be a minor variation on a familiar product.

“Chinese mahjong designs have barely changed for decades,” Zhu says. “American mahjong is completely different. A circle tile could be a football or a bunch of grapes. One grape stands for one dot, and nine grapes represent nine dots.”

American sets also include Arabic numerals and joker tiles, while familiar symbols are constantly reworked around seasonal themes and customers’ ideas. Summer collections feature seashells and aquatic plants; Christmas designs use Santa hats and trees.

And while traditional Chinese sets are usually molded from melamine in a narrow range of colors, American buyers prefer acrylic tiles with richer palettes, sometimes built from six or seven colored layers visible along the edge.

“Every customer wants their own concept,” Zhu says. “The color palettes are also much richer than those used in China.”

Chinese players, he says, tend to value weight, legibility, and how the tiles feel in the hand. American buyers, by contrast, want sets distinctive enough to display and expressive enough to reflect their tastes.

“I gradually understood that they weren’t just buying mahjong to play mahjong,” Zhu says. “A lot of the time, they’re buying a lifestyle.”

Factory reset

Inside Zhu’s factory, traditional Chinese mahjong and its American reinvention sit side by side. Dust-covered melamine slabs are stacked near the entrance, while baskets of brightly colored acrylic tiles and export cartons crowd the corridors beyond.

By 4 p.m., Zhu is usually outside the workshop, surrounded by cardboard boxes as he seals packages and confirms overseas delivery addresses with couriers. He moves between the packing area and loading site until sunset.

After the workers leave, he returns to his office to answer inquiries that accumulated during the afternoon. His wife stays at the UV printer, often working until midnight.

At 7 a.m. the next day, Zhu unlocks the factory gate and starts again.

For years, inquiries from new buyers came weeks or even months apart. Orders from Zhu’s long-term domestic clients remained steady, but rising material costs and intensifying competition had squeezed profits. To keep costs down, he and his wife took on work once handled by employees.

Now, he receives dozens of inquiries every day — from foreign trade companies, Amazon sellers, independent online retailers, and buyers on Alibaba.

“I used to make just 20 sets of American mahjong a year,” he says. “Now, I can turn out 200 sets a day.”

Unlike traditional Chinese sets, which can be reproduced using fixed molds, each American order requires new adjustments to engraving, printing, and coloring. A batch of 300 to 400 acrylic sets takes 15 to 20 days to complete — three to five days longer than the same number of Chinese sets.

“People buy them the way they buy clothes,” Zhu says. “What’s fashionable this year may be completely different next year.”

To keep up, Zhu has invested another 1 million yuan ($148,000) in laser engravers, UV printers, and other equipment. But he has hired only two or three additional workers, leaving his family to absorb much of the extra labor.

At the center of the workshop, a giant white sack hangs above a mound of acrylic tiles. Zhu’s parents, both in their 80s, sit on opposite sides of the pile, lifting the pieces one by one and arranging them into neat rows, every face turned in the same direction. Their hands move with a steady, practiced rhythm.

They work from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., the same hours as the factory’s other employees.

“I can do 100 sets a day,” Zhu’s father says. “Workers’ wages aren’t cheap. At least the two of us can save a few hundred yuan.”

A few steps away, Jin Guihua, 62, sorts black tiles before they are colored. Their engraved patterns are barely visible against the dark surface, so she lifts each rack toward the window, tilting it until the light catches the shallow lines.

She scans the rows for matching designs, tapping each selected tile against the edge of the table before setting it aside. Sometimes she checks more than five tiles before finding the next match.

Jin once sorted about 150 sets a day. The smaller tiles and changing patterns of American mahjong have reduced her output to about 60.

“The designs are more complicated and harder to identify,” she says.

Brand new

This past March, five young entrepreneurs arrived in Taixing to start a mahjong business.

A few minutes from Zhu’s family-run factory, they turned a village house into a workshop. Machines occupied the ground floor; their bedrooms were upstairs. There were no fixed hours or weekends.

Between them, the five had experience in sales, technology, and international trade. None had ever made a mahjong tile.



Li Mingzhi, 30, leads the venture, which operates under the name SenJoy Mahjong. A former Alibaba employee, he saw American mahjong as a chance to sell a higher-value product overseas. He recruited his former colleague Wang Hao, his younger brother, and several childhood friends from northwestern China’s Gansu province to build the venture.

“I never imagined I’d move to such a remote village to start a business,” says Wang, 28.

Zhu estimates that nearly 30 new factories have sprung up in Taixing over the past year as entrepreneurs rush into American mahjong. The town’s fragmented supply chain has allowed outsiders to enter without building a factory from scratch.

“Here, you don’t need to build an entire production line yourself,” Li tells Sixth Tone. “You can outsource each step and focus on design and branding.”

In practice, however, the workshop became a crash course in manufacturing.

“Every day is unpredictable,” Li says. “Customers can call at any time, and problems can emerge at every stage — production, design, communication, quality inspection. Working until 3 or 4 a.m. is normal.”

The new equipment offered precision but no ready-made solution for mahjong production: sizes varied, hand-cut pieces did not match machine-cut ones, and every fault required another round of testing.

“Almost every step brought a different problem,” Wang says.

The UV printer proved especially difficult. Each design had to be aligned by hand, and a shift of just 1 millimeter could push the ink outside the engraved lines.

The night before Sixth Tone’s visit, all five stayed up until 3 a.m. trying to solve the problem. “Before entering the industry, I thought making mahjong would be simple,” says Wang. “Once I started, I realized American sets are closer to handicrafts.”

Despite the setbacks, the team produced and sold about 1,000 sets in its first few months, generating roughly 230,000 yuan in sales. Its customers included businesses selling on Amazon.

Li put 1.5 million yuan of his own savings into the venture. “Based on our current orders,” says Li, “we expect the business to recover that investment within six months.”

To avoid becoming another contract manufacturer in Taixing’s crowded supply chain, the team began working with outside designers to develop original sets. It also launched an independent website and overseas social media accounts.

“For us, building a brand starts with original design,” Li says. “We might become the first company in Taixing — and perhaps one of the first in China — to build a real mahjong brand instead of simply manufacturing for others.”

The team hopes to reach buyers directly through social media, influencers, online sellers, and brick-and-mortar retailers.

Their bestseller uses a coral-reef theme. Against a shimmering blue base, coral motifs represent bamboo tiles, shells stand in for circles, and small fish serve as jokers.

“As long as the designs aren’t ugly, we’re not worried about sales,” Li says. “Right now, demand far exceeds supply.”

Wang is more cautious. Today’s buyers, he says, remain a relatively small group with strong spending power. If American mahjong reaches a broader market, more manufacturers will follow, he says, adding: “Price wars are unavoidable.”

Hua, one of the first Chinese traders to bet on American mahjong, has watched competitors multiply within months.

When she launched the business, Hua handled every part of the operation herself, often staying up late to respond to customers in the U.S. and sleeping as little as two hours a night. Today, her Ningbo-based company employs about 10 people and provides customer service around the clock.

But the market that once seemed wide open has become more crowded. Designs that once sold out quickly are now easier to source, and more suppliers are competing for the same orders.

“The conversion rate isn’t as good as before,” Hua says. Her sales data show that fewer visitors become inquiries, and fewer inquiries turn into confirmed orders.

“The profit margins were much higher in the beginning, but now they have dropped significantly,” she says. “I think this is probably an inevitable stage for any viral product.”

She, too, has started developing designs of her own.

Last month, she began experimenting with AI to create early concepts before working with freelance designers to refine them. Her first ideas included themes inspired by witches, tennis, flowers, and Christmas.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Workers sort uncarved and unpainted mahjong tiles at Zhu Ronggen’s factory in Taixing, Jiangsu province, June 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.title: Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018855/Chinese Rafting Park in Hot Water Over ‘Female Companion’ Service
World.content:
A river rafting tourist attraction in southwestern China has come under fire for offering “temporary girlfriends” and “very attractive” female companions who hold hands with, hug, and kiss customers while they raft.

Reported widely last week, the female companion service was offered by Luobei River Drifting, a popular rafting attraction in Guizhou province, beginning this summer. The rafting route, known for its thrilling rapids, lasts between 1.5 and 4 hours and covers up to 12.5 kilometers. Tickets cost up to 238 yuan ($35) per person.

In recent years, rafting attractions around China, including in the central Henan province, the eastern Jiangsu province, and the southern Hainan province, have launched scripted “NPC” rafting experiences, hiring workers to act as wolves, monkeys, bears, and frogs, as well as characters from the classic novel “Journey to the West” while customers raft. Related videos on Chinese social media have garnered tens of thousands of likes.

An undercover reporter at High Wind News, a platform under state-run media outlet Chinese Business View, posing as a customer contacted the attraction’s customer service on the messaging app WeChat, which informed them that they could choose from three service packages: a 398-yuan “highly attractive” companion who accompanies the rider with no additional physical contact, a 1,288-yuan partner with “upgraded appearance with polite physical contact,” and a 1,988-yuan “temporary girlfriend” option.

Customer service sent the reporter several photos — purported to be real pictures of the female companions — along with profiles of more than 30 women, including their height, weight, and age. Some photos were labeled “pure green,” indicating the companion’s service does not include “sexual behavior or contact.”

“The 1,988-yuan package is just like dating — you can hold hands, hug, and kiss,” the staff member told the undercover reporter, hinting that there could be further meetups after the initial rafting encounter.

“We create a legitimate setting for you to meet and communicate. We’re essentially just the intermediary,” the customer service representative added, claiming to receive around 400 groups of customers a day. The staff member also said the rafting park had more than 1,000 workers and required companions to be reserved in advance.

An account on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by the name of “Luobei River NPC Scripted Drifting” had reportedly posted promotional videos of young women accompanying tourists during rafting and water activities, with slogans such as, “What heals you isn’t the scenery, but the emotional value.” The account has since been deleted.

Employees at the tourist attraction later confirmed to domestic media that companion services were available and directed reporters to the same customer service WeChat account.

In an official announcement posted on WeChat last Thursday, however, the company behind the park denied any connection to the female companion service, saying a separate company had privately launched the service.

A day later, on July 31, the local tourism bureau announced that Luobei River Drifting had agreed to collaborate with a management company specializing in upgraded rafting experiences, where tourists become the protagonists in stories instead of passive sightseers. According to the company’s official WeChat account, it had signed the cooperation agreement on May 6.

On July 31, the rafting operator was ordered by the local government to suspend operations for “rectification.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Female rafting companions. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.title: Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018854/Check in, Log on, Stay for Months: Life at China’s 9-Cent Internet Café
World.content:
Outside an unassuming three-story building in downtown Kangyi Town, in the eastern Shandong province, hangs a sign that reads: “Striving to be the cheapest internet café in China.”

With charges as low as 0.6 yuan ($0.09) an hour, it’s certainly not false advertising. Yet step inside and you will find not just gamers chasing rock-bottom prices, but also a mix of locals and out-of-towners with myriad tales of misfortune, many looking to rise from their own rock bottom.

Here, customers can bathe and do laundry for free, enjoy a lunch of meat and vegetables for just 10 yuan, and even sleep in reclining esports chairs. For those looking to get back on their feet, it’s the ultimate low-to-no-cost option.

Like many of its patrons, the café’s owner, Wang Zhongkai, is also just trying to survive. After struggling to keep the doors open for more than a decade, the 38-year-old decided to slash his prices last year to attract more foot traffic.

The move certainly accomplished that — although it’s also inadvertently created a shelter for people in hard times.

After seeing a video about the internet café on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, Wang’s first out-of-town customer traveled 800 kilometers from neighboring Jiangsu province to “seek refuge” — and ended up staying for eight months.

Changing fortunes

China had roughly 122,600 licensed internet cafés last year, up 12% from 2024, according to the Internet Access Service Association of China. However, data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism shows that average annual revenue fell from 216,000 yuan to 197,000 yuan over that same period.

Hardware is the biggest investment. With ever-changing technology, a new computer costing 15,000 yuan can lose a third of its value within a year, with software requiring constant paid-for upgrades.

Wang’s is one of only two surviving internet cafés in Kangyi. The business today has more than 150 computers of various specs, including 35 priced at 0.6 yuan an hour. The other machines in the main hall range from 0.9 yuan to 3 yuan an hour, while private one-person rooms are available for 99 yuan a day.

From nearly empty every day, Wang has seen occupancy increase to about 90%. At nighttime, the second floor is illuminated by the shifting colors of the PC screens, with the faces of customers — almost entirely men — aglow with yellow, green, red, and blue hues. Some are fast asleep, wrapped in summer blankets, headphones dangling from their neck.

Over the years, Wang, a father of three, has tried many ways to increase his income. He tried opening a grocery store on the side, which saw him lose 500,000 yuan in about six months. To recover, in 2023, he moved to Beijing — leaving his wife in charge of the café — to become a daijia, a designated driver for hire, working 15 hours a day. One day, he was so exhausted that he fell asleep while riding his electric bike and crashed.

He knows all too well that sometimes people just need to get through a rough patch. While living in the capital, he would pay 15 yuan to spend the night at an internet café where he could charge his e-bike and get hot water.

Wang returned to Kangyi in 2025. Today he helps his customers find low-cost rooms in town for as little as 200 yuan a month, with no deposit. For those who can’t even afford that, he lets them sleep for free in the café’s luxurious esports chairs.

He also advertises day-labor gigs available nearby, such as sorting packages at a courier depot or casual shifts at a machinery plant. Most of his customers decline, however, either because they’re not fit enough to handle manual labor or can’t stomach the idea of being bossed around.

His wife and mother-in-law are responsible for preparing lunch every day at the café, with one meat dish, one vegetable dish, and mountains of rice and steamed buns. Most diners pay 10 yuan, but those without a penny eat for free.

The showers and an industrial-size washing machine are also free to use — Wang even provides soap and detergent.

Despite the increased foot traffic, Wang’s profit margins remain wafer-thin. He says his family has invested more than 700,000 yuan in new computers, yet their revenue streams comprise only the cut-rate internet fees, sales of food and drink, and the occasional livestream on Douyin, during which some viewers will send virtual gifts. Except for relatives, the business has only one employee — an elderly male cleaner.

Boosting opportunities

Qiang Yu, a 30-something from Huaibei in the eastern Anhui province, has spent every day and night in the “0.6-yuan zone” for nearly a year. Like many others here, he makes money as a “game booster,” which involves playing video games to level up someone else’s account. His specialty is the online role-playing game Legend of Mir 2.

High-level accounts in popular games are worth tens of thousands of yuan, and cheating can lead to a permanent ban by game developers. Account owners are usually unwilling to hand their username and password to strangers, but Wang has built a reputation among several clients, offering a personal guarantee for any losses. He regularly farms out orders to the boosters at his internet café — and doesn’t even take a cut.

In the past, Qiang did manual jobs — digging gravel by the railway tracks, getting paid by the meter, his hands raw and blistered at the end of a shift, as well as toiling at factories making garments, lights, and electronics. It left him with a “crushing depression,” he says.

Qiang now earns just over 100 yuan for 12 hours’ work and survives on just 25 yuan a day. If, in a year, he has 10,000 yuan in his pocket, he plans to go home and clear the weeds that have taken over his courtyard.

Cao Ti Lie, a gamer who asked to be identified only by his username, arrived in Kangyi from Foshan, in the southern Guangdong province, in June. He grew up in video arcades, and now regularly livestreams to 60,000 subscribers on Douyin as he competes in the classic King of Fighters ’97.

Gaming used to be fun, he says; now it’s a full-time job. “The heart of the boy I was is dead. When you have to face life, it gets erased.”

The 41-year-old previously ran a business in Foshan and was making 30,000 yuan a month, but bad investments and a gambling habit saw his debts pile up. His wife left with their children, and then his mother suffered a stroke and broke her hip, losing the ability to care for herself.

Soon after spotting a video about Wang’s internet café, he hopped on a train here. His only goal is to save enough money to cover the costs of his mother’s nursing home.

Future is now

Wang’s day starts at 8 a.m. He scrubs five toilets, restocks the fridge, wipes down the keyboards, picks up any trash from the night before, and then takes his spot at the front counter.

He sees plenty of local faces come and go, but many of the out-of-towners are now permanent fixtures. In February, the café hosted about 40 people on Chinese New Year’s Eve, an important day on the calendar for family reunion.

Mao Lifen, a gamer from the northern Shanxi province who arrived in May, says he tries not to think about the future. He used to have a plan — work at a factory for five years, save up, and open a fruit shop. This was derailed when he and his colleagues had a falling out with the factory management and quit.

He went to work in food delivery and partnered with a friend to open a restaurant, maxing out several credit cards to the tune of 100,000 yuan and losing it all. Mao then tried starting a business with another friend, who ran off with all their money. A string of bad investments appears to have killed his interest in making plans.

His only thought now is to get through this year. “I’ve got food and drink — what is there to be unhappy about?” he says. At Wang’s internet café, he takes boosting orders for the first-person tactical shooter game Delta Force. When he’s not playing, he likes to walk up to the rooftop to look at the trees in the distance.

Mao likes this life that requires next to no human contact: everyone stares at their screen, submerged in the game. With his headphones on, there is no “outside world.”

This year, a wannabe entrepreneur from out of town visited Wang with a view to copying his business model elsewhere. Wang laid it out for him: 150 computers plus renovations, licensing, and other expenses mean at least 2 million yuan upfront; profits will unlikely keep pace with the equipment’s depreciation; and a minimum of three or four employees are needed to run 24/7. The visitor listened patiently and immediately abandoned the plan.

Wang knows he’s too deep into the industry to pull out. When he was young, he dreamed of making a fortune and owning a luxury car, but now “I know my limits,” he says. With a 30-year mortgage and still owing 110,000 yuan for equipment, his only wish is to draw customers and stay afloat.

(For privacy reasons, Qiang Yu and Mao Lifen are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Jiang Wanru.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Customers sleep in the esports chairs, at Wang’s internet café in Kangyi Town, June 2026. Jiang Wanru/White Night Workshop)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.title: A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018850/A Chinese Coal City Finds New Use for Old Mines: Cooling Homes
World.content:
A Chinese city has launched a new residential cooling program using water from abandoned coal mines, a low-carbon initiative that could replace traditional air conditioners.

The initiative in the eastern Jiangsu province’s city of Xuzhou routes water from the now-defunct Woniushan Coal Mine to apartments in a nearby neighborhood, domestic media reported this week. The water maintains a consistent temperature of 19 degrees Celsius year-round.

Disused mines often fill with water via rainwater accumulation and groundwater seepage — water that can then be used to heat or cool nearby homes.

Xuzhou, a former coal-producing center with a decades-long mining history, has previously used abandoned mine water for clean heating, including a system installed last winter at its former Hanqiao Coal Mine. With annual average temperatures climbing and China’s “dual carbon” initiative — where the country aims to peak its carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 — a national priority, the cooling initiative, which began June 1, has been a focus for the city.

“After heat exchange (with the homes), the water returns to the mine, without having consumed any energy or produced any carbon emissions,” Zhang Tao, leader of the cooling project and a worker at Xukuang Heating Company, told state media outlet CCTV. Compared with traditional air conditioning, he said, this technology lowers carbon emissions and aligns more closely with China’s energy conservation and emission reduction policy.

According to domestic media, such closed-loop geothermal systems reduce energy consumption by approximately 50% compared with traditional methods. It is also estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions for the 100 homes in the pilot program by about 50 tons annually.

The city offered residents in the pilot program two free months of cooling, after which they’ll be charged quarterly at 4 yuan ($0.60) per square meter.

Wang, a resident in the pilot area, said that in previous summers her monthly electricity bill often exceeded 400 yuan due to air conditioner usage. In contrast, the pilot program has allowed her to cool her home for four months this summer for only 410 yuan. She said her home now maintains a constant temperature 24 hours a day, and the system is quiet, unlike air conditioners.

Zhang, the heating company researcher, noted the great potential of the pilot program. “This year we only used a part of Woniushan Coal Mine’s capacity, and since the mine has significant potential, in the future we plan on using it to capacity, extending it to more neighborhoods.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.content:
LIVE

The multitalented artist talks about her decision to step into her new persona as Leanne, her work as an actress, and what else she has in store for her fans

MANILA, Philippines – Most people first encounter Leanne Mamonong as one-half of the duo Leanne and Naara, as the soloist barb., or even as Mihan from the film Open Endings.

This time, though, she’s marking a whole new chapter in her career where she makes music under her own name for the very first time — making her debut with the single “Babaero,” a reimagination of the ’80s Randy Santiago hit.

The multitalented artist sits down with multimedia reporter Juno Reyes to talk about her decision to step into her new persona as Leanne, her work as an actress, and what else she has in store for her fans. Watch until the end for a special performance!

World.title: Long shot? Filipino teen takes swing at Major League Baseball dreams
World.content:
As lofty as the MLB dream may be for Filipinos, 13-year-old Ateneo high school baseball standout Aiden Lazaro looks to be on the right path

No homegrown Filipino has reached Major League Baseball.

Sure, there is Claudio Manela, a pitcher from Cavite whose Negro League stint with the Cincinnati Cuban Stars in the 1920s is now recognized as part of MLB history.

There is also Bobby Chouinard, who holds the distinction as the first player born in the Philippines to see action in the MLB since its racial integration in 1947 when he made his debut for the Oakland Athletics in 1996.

Several players of Filipino heritage have made it to the MLB as well, including current New York Yankees shortstop Anthony Volpe, three-time World Series champion and two-time Cy Young Award winner Tim Lincecum, former Cincinnati Redlegs outfielder Bobby Balcena, former San Francisco Giants pitcher Geno Espineli, and former Florida Marlins outfielder Chris Aguila.

Aiden Lazaro, a 13-year-old standout from Ateneo high school, hopes to break new ground for the country.

“My biggest dream is of course to play in the MLB, to get drafted by a team and to hopefully play in the majors,” Lazaro told Rappler.

As lofty as that dream may be, Lazaro looks to be on the right path.

Lazaro won the Most Runs Batted In (RBIs) honors when he represented the Philippines in the 2024 U-12 Asian Baseball Championship in Japan, and then a year later, helped National Capital Region capture the gold medal in the 2025 Palarong Pambansa in Ilocos Norte.

Starting his baseball journey at the age of five, Lazaro also made Ateneo’s juniors roster for the UAAP last year, becoming the only Grade 7 student to earn a spot.

Those accomplishments have led to Lazaro being accepted to IMG Academy, a renowned private sports-focused boarding school and training center in Florida, United States, which has produced around 150 students who were drafted to a professional league in the last 10 years.

Some of IMG Academy’s most notable alumni include tennis icons Serena Williams and Maria Sharapova, golf champion Nelly Korda, and NBA players Dwight Powell and Zach Edey.

And it also helps that Lazaro has the unwavering support of his mother Shelly, who accompanied him to the United States for the first phase of his athletic development program at IMG Academy.

“I really love the training there as I was able to train with very top-tier coaches and play with very good players. After the training, I was feeling very proud of myself that I was able to train, take lessons from very good coaches and play with very good teammates from the US,” Lazaro said.

‘Long shot’

While Shelly believes in Aiden, she also recognizes that making the MLB is a “long shot,” especially for a player coming from a country where baseball remains in the shadows of more popular sports.

That perspective prompted Shelly to temper her son’s expectations as he embarked on his training at IMG Academy.

“When you ask all baseball players, all of them dream to get to the MLB. It’s everyone’s dream. For Filipinos and for Asians, it’s really a long shot. I’m not delusional or I don’t have all these fantasies. My goal is to really just support Aiden,” said Shelly.

“My dream for Aiden, and I will support him all the way, is for him to reach the farthest that this skill, passion, and potential can realistically take him. Wherever it may take him, whether it’s the MLB or… the farthest that he’s meant to achieve, based on what he’s got.”

SUPPORT. Aiden Lazaro with his mother Shelly. Photo from Shelly Lazaro Facebook page

But Shelly’s optimism grew as Aiden received glowing feedback from IMG Academy coaches.

Local coaches, according to Shelly, describe Aiden as a player who is advanced for his age. Those from the IMG Academy share the same view.

“When I was hearing that and I was hearing all these feedback from the coaches, in my mind, ‘Oh, so it’s not a remote possibility. Oh there’s hope.’ Kind of made me really excited of what’s going to happen next. It’s still a long journey. It really gave me hope, seeing him train there and seeing how the coaches objectively evaluated his skills and his commitment.”

Firm belief

Aiden considers himself capable of playing any position, but he mainly plays catcher and shortstop.

And he patterns his game after some of the best in the history of the sport, including legendary Puerto Rican catcher Yadier Molina, a two-time World Series champion during his 19-year stint with the St. Louis Cardinals; current Los Angeles Dodgers catcher Will Smith, a three-time World Series winner; and current Kansas City Royals ace shortstop Bobby Witt Jr, a two-time Gold Glove and two-time Silver Slugger awardee.

Curiously, the catching coach at IMG Academy — according to Shelly — sees a lot of Molina in Aiden.

“That’s the first time I heard the name Molina, because the coach said… ‘You know Aiden, it’s really up to you. You can go as far as you would want to take yourself. It’s really up to you.’ It’s really up to him. If he wants to be in the MLB, he can make it to MLB, for as long as he doesn’t stop training, he doesn’t stop working hard,” Shelly said.

Although he knows he still has a long way to go, Aiden trusts in his ability to get where he wants to be.

“I agree with my mom that I’ll try my best to get as far as I can with my skills, but I also think that it could be possible, especially with the opportunities and resources given,” he said.

“In the future, I can imagine, and hopefully, that I will be playing at the college-slash-D1 level or even playing already in the MLB, perhaps the Triple-A or Double-A.”

Aiden has returned to the country to continue his studies at Ateneo as a Grade 8 student, but he will keep on working with IMG Academy under a hybrid setup.

“He loves representing the school and the Philippines. So we’re lucky that we have that option. For the time being, he will still be doing the academics here, he will still be a student of Ateneo,” said Shelly.

“School break, holiday, at least a two-week vacation that’s not going to be in conflict with any local tournaments, school, stuff like that, we fly. So we will be really shuttling between Manila and Florida.” – Rappler.com

World.title: How Jollibee became Filipino food’s biggest ambassador in the US
World.content:
MORE JOLLIBEE BRANCHES. Fast-food chain Jollibee opens a new branch in San Francisco, Los Angeles in the United States on August 5, 2026.

Jollibee’s North American boom shows how Filipino food and culture are finding a bigger audience beyond the diaspora

NEW YORK, USA – When Jollibee opened the doors to its first store in Manhattan, New York City in 2018, customers arrived in droves.

They braved the rain. A few came dressed as the restaurant’s iconic red bee mascot. Others claimed to have waited in line for over 20 hours.

The Eighth Avenue location, located near Times Square, was Jollibee’s 41st store in North America, and the first of three branches in New York City.

In just six years, the homegrown Filipino fast-food chain would more than double its number of stores in North America and establish a fanbase that rivals the likes of McDonald’s and KFC.

New York City resident Daniel Kim visited Jollibee’s flagship Times Square location with his fiancée, Izzie Penn. Kim, who moved to New York from Metro Manila for school two years ago, said that he eats at Jollibee when he’s missing home and craves Filipino food.

He noted from his visits that the restaurant was usually packed with a mix of Filipino and non-Filipino customers.

“It’s the Filipino restaurant that has the most clout outside of the Philippines,” he said. “When I first came into the Jollibee, I expected all the customers to be Filipino, but I was pleasantly surprised to see that there were a lot of different people.”

The company currently operates over 100 stores in North America and plans to reach 500 stores by 2030, according to a company press release issued last year.

Its rapid expansion comes at a time of increasing interest in Filipino culture and media abroad, from tennis player Alex Eala’s historic Washington Open win, music groups Bini and SB19’s surging global popularity, and the recent ube craze.

With the Philippines in the spotlight, experts say now is the best time for Jollibee to continue to grow and serve as a cultural ambassador for the country.

“Jollibee has the momentum and the wind in its sails at this moment,” said Ty Matejowsky, a food scholar and anthropology professor at the University of Central Florida. “They’ve shown that they can go toe to toe in international markets. I really feel like they will, if not achieve the 500-store goal, then get pretty close.”

Buzzy beginnings

Jollibee was founded by current Jollibee Foods Corporation chairman Tony Tan Caktiong in 1975 as an ice-cream-selling business before morphing in 1978 into the fast-food brand it is known as today.

It has seen exponential growth over the decades, landing a spot as one of the Philippines’ top 100 corporations in 1987, debuting on the Philippine Stock Exchange in 1993, and eventually becoming the dominant fast-food chain in the country. It took its ambitions abroad and opened its first US store in Daly City, California, in 1998.

Almost 30 years later, Jollibee shows no signs of slowing down its North American expansion. On Friday, it opened its Downtown San Francisco branch — an occasion celebrated by the Philippine Consulate General in San Francisco, San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, and members of the Filipino American community.

“This dynamic city is a milestone location for us as we continue to accelerate our growth across California,” said Beth de la Cruz, president of Jollibee North America, in a press release.

Matejowsky credited Jollibee’s ability to break into the American fast-food space to “diaspora marketing.” The approach involved catering to communities that had ties to the Philippines, such as those on the West Coast with a large population of Filipinos and overseas Filipino workers. As a result, Jollibee had a built-in market of customers who were already familiar with the brand and its offerings.

Catering to American tastes

Still, the company sought to broaden its appeal beyond the Filipino diaspora. Reporting by Bloomberg last year showed that 60% of Jollibee’s customers in the US are non-Filipino.

According to Matejowsky, Jollibee’s success with American customers can be partly ascribed to the popularity of its signature chicken dish, Chickenjoy.

Last month, USA Today named Jollibee the number one fast-food fried chicken for the third consecutive year. It earned this achievement through popular vote.

The company has also made efforts to win over American customers by tweaking its menu. While it kept local favorites like its peach mango pie, palabok and famously sweet-tasting Jolly Spaghetti, it also began to offer biscuits as a side at some locations.

Kim said while he wishes Jollibee’s American branches offered set meals with rice like they do in the Philippines, he thinks its dishes are still able to retain their familiar taste.

“They’ve done a good job keeping the spirit of Filipino food, while also changing to the needs of an American market,” he said. “Just look at their menu. What American hates chicken tenders? What American doesn’t like hamburgers?”

Another component in Jollibee’s recipe for success, Matejowsky said, is social media and the power of reputation.

Izzie Penn, Kim’s fiancée who hails from Texas, said that she knew of Jollibee before she even visited it through content she saw online.

“I would hear about it through YouTube sometimes. I would be like, ‘Oh, Jollibee, that’s the Filipino chicken place,’” Penn said. She also mentioned seeing videos of the mascot dancing on social media, which made the brand memorable to her.

Along with Jollibee’s outsized social media presence, Matejowsky described a strong general interest in Asian food and culture in the US as a boost to its success. He pointed to the spread of boba tea shops in the country and said he saw Jollibee’s popularity as a sign of Filipino culture getting its time in the sun.

“It feels like many of the other cuisines of Southeast Asia, like Vietnamese food and Thai food, had their moments, and it was always kind of disappointing for Filipino food not to have that,” he said. “But now I think you can readily see that it’s meeting the moment.” – Rappler.com

Erika is a Rappler intern based in the United States. She is taking up a Master’s degree in political and foreign affairs journalism at Northwestern University. She has finished internship programs at CNBC, CNN, and Capitol News Illinois, where she did articles related to business and technology.

World.title: Taste mee pok, otak-otak, octopus adobo at Grand Hyatt’s buffet for a limited time
World.content:
LIMITED. Mee pok, otak-otak, and octopus adobo will be served for a limited time at Grand Hyatt's Grand Kitchen buffet.

MANILA, Philippines – Grand Hyatt Manila’s usual buffet spread has three new additions for diners looking to try something different: mee pok, otak-otak, and octopus adobo.

The dishes are part of Culinary Connections, a limited collaboration among Singapore Airlines, Mastercard, and Grand Hyatt Manila running at The Grand Kitchen in Bonifacio Global City from August 6 to October 5.
